Farewill is a private company that provides will-writing, probate, and cremation services in the UK, based in London. Founded in 2015. It claims to be the UK's biggest will writer. Farewill is registered in England and Wales with the Law Society and was declared the National Will Writing Firm of the year in 2019.

It is a B2C product but is also provided as a free service through several charities.

History
Farewill was founded in 2015 by Dan Garrett (Co-Founder & CEO) and Tom Rogers (Co-Founder & CPTO). Garrett started the company after being inspired whilst designing new products for elderly residents in a care home in Tokyo.

Dan Garrett returned to the UK and moved into the death industry, where he organised 15 funerals and gained a qualification in will writing, founding Farewill on July 24, 2015 to "make [death care] easier".

In 2016, following their seed funding round, Tracy Doree, angel investor and founder of venture capital firm Kindred Capital, joined Farewill as its Chairperson. In addition to Tracy, the company has 3 additional Directors: Tom Rogers, its Chief Product and Technology Officer (CPTO), Tim Levene of Augmentum Fintech and Dan Garrett, the CEO.

In 2019, Farewill was listed as one of Rocketlist's Top 20 Companies to Work For, Fintech50's Hottest Fintechs to watch, and Sifted's Top UK Startups to follow in 2020. It was awarded best social innovation at the Europas in 2020.

According to Augmentum Fintech, Farewill grew by 10x between January 2019 and July 2020. Like many other unprofitable tech startups, Farewill announced redundancies in 2022.

Farewill's position in the death industry and work with charities has been a topic of discussion due to Farewill's unregulated status. Farewill's CEO has criticized the sector as “overtly traditional”, with prices that are “unaffordably high”. In 2020, the Financial Times questioned the need for new technology in this sector.

Services

Direct
Farewill offers a number of services, including will-writing (online and over the phone), a direct cremation service, a probate service, and a subscription-based will update service.

Farewill states that users can complete an online will in 15 minutes for £90. An additional service, at £10 per year allows for the same will to be updated an unlimited number of times. The will-writing process is based on questions that the user answers to provide the necessary information. After this, the user goes through a payment process, and then they can download and sign the document in the presence of their chosen witnesses to finally obtain their legal will.

Direct cremations - where the cremation happens privately and the ashes are returned to the family afterwards - start from £980. This has been reported as being around a third of the UK average cost for direct cremation, and around a fifth of the average UK funeral cost.

In 2016, TechCrunch wrote of their data privacy concerns of storing wills digitally, online. This led to Farewill responding that user data is stored on Amazon's Secure Storage Service in Ireland and encrypted using AES-256 encryption.

Charity partners
The company has partnered with 50 UK charities, including Cancer Research UK, British Heart Foundation, McMillan, The Royal British Legion, and Christian Aid. The charities provide access to the will-writing service to encourage bequeathals to their organisation.

It is estimated that this has generated over £260 million in pledged income, across the charities, since Farewill launched.

CEO – Dan Garrett
Dan Garrett is the chief executive officer and co-founder of Farewill. He completed an MSc in Design at the Royal College of Art, a Master of Structural Engineering at Oxford University, and an MSc in Global Innovation Design at Imperial College London.

Schema Migration Log for the Inventario Nacional de Bienes Culturales Database Kept by the data team of the Ministerio de Cultura del Perú. Each entry records a migration applied to the production database
 that stores records of archaeological objects, colonial artworks and historic buildings, together with the reason for it. Migrations are numbered sequentially and applied with Flyway.

Migration 087, applied 14 February 2026

- Added a geometry column for site boundaries using PostGIS, replacing the single point coordinate. - Created a spatial index on the new column. - Backfilled boundaries for 1,240 archaeological sites from shapefiles provided by regional directorates. Many archaeological sites, such as the adobe complexes on the north coast, cover several hectares, and a single point could not show whether a proposed construction project overlapped with them. Municipal offices reque
sted the change after a road project near Chan Chan was approved because its route passed 300 metres from the registered point but cut through the actual site. Sites without boundary data keep their point coordinate until regional teams submit polygons. Migration 086, applied 30 January 2026 - Split the owner column into owner type and owner reference. - Added a foreign key from owner reference to the new institutions table. Before this change, the owner field contained free text, with the same museum spelled in more than a dozen ways, for example Museo Larco, Museo Arqueológico Rafael Larco Herrera and Larco Museum. Data analyst Renzo Castañeda cleaned roughly 18,000 records and matched them to 2,310 institutions. Private owners are now stored wit
h a reference to a separate protected table to comply with the personal data protection law. Migration 085, applied 9 January 2026 - Converted all text columns from LATIN1 to UTF-8.
- Rebuilt full-text search indexes with the Spanish dictionary. The database was created in 2008 with LATIN1 encoding, which could not represent some characters used in Quechua and Aymara names of sites and objects, such as apostrophes marking glottal stops in certain orthographies. The conversion required a maintenance window of four hours and was tested twice on a copy of production. After the change, searches for words with accents also return results typed without them. Migration 084, applied 12 December 2025

- Dropped the unused legacy column condition code.

This column had been replaced in 2019 by a structured condition assessment table but remained in the schema, confusing new developers. Before dropping it, we confirmed with the conservation department that no reports still used it. Process Notes Every migrati
on is reviewed by at least two team members and tested in staging against a full copy of production data. Head of data, Gabriela Rojas, approves all migrations that alter or remove columns.

Schema Migration Log for the Inventario Nacional de Bienes Culturales Database

Kept by the data team of the Ministerio de Cultura del Perú. Each entry records a migration applied to the production database that stores records of archaeological objects, colonial artworks and historic buildings, together with the reason for it. Migrations are numbered sequentially and applied with Flyway.

Migration 087, applied 14 February 2026

- Added a geometry column for site boundaries using PostGIS, replacing the single point coordinate.
- Created a spatial index on the new column.
- Backfilled boundaries for 1,240 archaeological sites from shapefiles provided by regional directorates.

Many archaeological sites, such as the adobe complexes on the north coast, cover several hectares, and a single point could not show whether a proposed construction project overlapped with them. Municipal offices requested the change after a road project near Chan Chan was approved because its route passed 300 metres from the registered point but cut through the actual site. Sites without boundary data keep their point coordinate until regional teams submit polygons.

Migration 086, applied 30 January 2026

- Split the owner column into owner type and owner reference.
- Added a foreign key from owner reference to the new institutions table.

Before this change, the owner field contained free text, with the same museum spelled in more than a dozen ways, for example Museo Larco, Museo Arqueológico Rafael Larco Herrera and Larco Museum. Data analyst Renzo Castañeda cleaned roughly 18,000 records and matched them to 2,310 institutions. Private owners are now stored with a reference to a separate protected table to comply with the personal data protection law.

Migration 085, applied 9 January 2026

- Converted all text columns from LATIN1 to UTF-8.
- Rebuilt full-text search indexes with the Spanish dictionary.

The database was created in 2008 with LATIN1 encoding, which could not represent some characters used in Quechua and Aymara names of sites and objects, such as apostrophes marking glottal stops in certain orthographies. The conversion required a maintenance window of four hours and was tested twice on a copy of production. After the change, searches for words with accents also return results typed without them.

Migration 084, applied 12 December 2025

- Dropped the unused legacy column condition code.

This column had been replaced in 2019 by a structured condition assessment table but remained in the schema, confusing new developers. Before dropping it, we confirmed with the conservation department that no reports still used it.

Process Notes

Every migration is reviewed by at least two team members and tested in staging against a full copy of production data. Head of data, Gabriela Rojas, approves all migrations that alter or remove columns.

Cross-Border Coral Monitoring Network, Annual Coordination Meeting

Location: Datça, Muğla, hosted by the Datça-Bozburun Special Environmental Protection Area office. Date: 14 to 15 April 2026. Participants: Dr. Sinan Kalkan and Dr. Merve Uzun (Turkey), Dr. Despina Galanaki and Dr. Yorgos Liapis (Greece), Hasan Bilgili (protected area manager), and six volunteer dive leaders from Kos, Symi and Bodrum. Recorder: Merve Uzun. Opening Dr. Kalkan welcomed participants and noted that this was the network's fourth annual meeting and the first held in person since 2023. The network monitors 31 sites with 
coral assemblages on both sides of the Gulf of Gökova and the waters around Kos, Nisyros and Symi. Its main focus is the Mediterranean stony coral Cladocora caespitosa and red gorgonian forests on deeper rocky walls. Results From 2025 Dr. Galanaki presented a summary of the 2025 surveys. Following last summer's heatwave, partial mortality of Cladocora colonies above 15 metres reached an average of 44 perce
nt at Greek sites and 51 percent at Turkish sites. Colonies deeper than 25 metres were in much better condition. Dr. Liapis added that invasive lionfish were now recorded at every site south of Kos, up from 
about half of sites in 2023. Data Sharing Participants discussed differences in data formats between the two teams, which had delayed the joint analysis by several months. Dr. Uzun proposed using a common database structure based on the ReefWatch Aegean protocol, wh
ich both teams already partly use. Dr. Liapis agreed but noted that Greek data mus
t remain on servers in
 the EU under the funding rules of the Hellenic Centre for Marine Research. The group agreed that a shared server hosted in Greece, with full access for Turkish partners, would satisfy both requirements. Volunteer Training Dive leaders reported that volunteers find it hard to distinguish recently dead coral from
older dead skeletons covered in algae. Dive leader Eleni Soulioti from Symi suggested producing a photo identification guide in Turkish, Greek and English. Agreed Actions

1. Merve Uzun and Yorgos Liapis will draft the common database structure by 31 May. 2. The Greek team will set up the shared server by the end of June.
3. Despina Galanaki will lead production of the trilingual photo guide, with photos supplied by both teams, for distribution before the summer survey season. 4. All teams will deploy additional temperature loggers at 10 and 25 metres at six key sites before 1 June.
5. Hasan Bilgili will contact the provincial directorate about extending the summer anchoring ban to two additional bays near Bozburun. 6. A joint 
paper on heatwave impacts will be drafted by September, with Sinan Kalkan as coordinator. Closing Participants thanked the protected area office for hosting. The next meeting will be held on Kos in spring 2027, with an online check-in planned for October 2026 after the summer surveys are complete.

Cross-Border Coral Monitoring Network, Annual Coordination Meeting

Location: Datça, Muğla, hosted by the Datça-Bozburun Special Environmental Protection Area office. Date: 14 to 15 April 2026. Participants: Dr. Sinan Kalkan and Dr. Merve Uzun (Turkey), Dr. Despina Galanaki and Dr. Yorgos Liapis (Greece), Hasan Bilgili (protected area manager), and six volunteer dive leaders from Kos, Symi and Bodrum. Recorder: Merve Uzun.

Opening

Dr. Kalkan welcomed participants and noted that this was the network's fourth annual meeting and the first held in person since 2023. The network monitors 31 sites with coral assemblages on both sides of the Gulf of Gökova and the waters around Kos, Nisyros and Symi. Its main focus is the Mediterranean stony coral Cladocora caespitosa and red gorgonian forests on deeper rocky walls.

Results From 2025

Dr. Galanaki presented a summary of the 2025 surveys. Following last summer's heatwave, partial mortality of Cladocora colonies above 15 metres reached an average of 44 percent at Greek sites and 51 percent at Turkish sites. Colonies deeper than 25 metres were in much better condition. Dr. Liapis added that invasive lionfish were now recorded at every site south of Kos, up from about half of sites in 2023.

Data Sharing

Participants discussed differences in data formats between the two teams, which had delayed the joint analysis by several months. Dr. Uzun proposed using a common database structure based on the ReefWatch Aegean protocol, which both teams already partly use. Dr. Liapis agreed but noted that Greek data must remain on servers in the EU under the funding rules of the Hellenic Centre for Marine Research. The group agreed that a shared server hosted in Greece, with full access for Turkish partners, would satisfy both requirements.

Volunteer Training

Dive leaders reported that volunteers find it hard to distinguish recently dead coral from older dead skeletons covered in algae. Dive leader Eleni Soulioti from Symi suggested producing a photo identification guide in Turkish, Greek and English.

Agreed Actions

1. Merve Uzun and Yorgos Liapis will draft the common database structure by 31 May.
2. The Greek team will set up the shared server by the end of June.
3. Despina Galanaki will lead production of the trilingual photo guide, with photos supplied by both teams, for distribution before the summer survey season.
4. All teams will deploy additional temperature loggers at 10 and 25 metres at six key sites before 1 June.
5. Hasan Bilgili will contact the provincial directorate about extending the summer anchoring ban to two additional bays near Bozburun.
6. A joint paper on heatwave impacts will be drafted by September, with Sinan Kalkan as coordinator.

Closing

Participants thanked the protected area office for hosting. The next meeting will be held on Kos in spring 2027, with an online check-in planned for October 2026 after the summer surveys are complete.

Minutes: People Committee, Hiring Process Redesign Held on 2 October 2025 at the Kolozsvár headquarters of Nordvest Logistics SRL, room 3B, from 15:00 to 16:20. Present: Ildikó Szász (HR director, chair), Paul Ungureanu (operations), Hajnal Benedek (finan
ce), Andrei Rusu (legal), Zoltán Péter (warehouse supervisor, Turda site). Apologies: Corina Toma. Background

Ildikó summarised why the committee asked for a redesign in June. Time to hire for warehouse roles had reached 41 days, nearly twice

Migration Log: Moving the Hai Au Retail Order Database From MySQL 5.7 to PostgreSQL 16

This log records each stage of the migration of the order database for Hai Au Retail, a Vietnamese chain of 140 convenience stores, carried out by its internal platform team with consultants from Seoul. Each entry lists what was changed and why. It is intended for engineers maintaining the system after cutover.

Stage 4, Completed 27 September 2026

1. Switched all write traffic from MySQL to PostgreSQL during the planned maintenance window from 01:00 to 03:30.
2. Placed MySQL in read-only mode and kept it running for 14 days as a fallback.
3. Enabled logical replication from PostgreSQL to the analytics warehouse.
4. Removed the dual-write code from the order service.

Cutover took 2 hours 10 minutes, inside the planned window. The main delay came from validating row counts on the order lines table, which holds about 410 million rows. Lead engineer Nguyen Ba Thanh decided to compare checksums on a sample of partitions rather than the full table to stay within the window, and full validation ran afterward with no differences found. MySQL is kept read-only so that the team can roll back quickly if a serious problem appears during the first fortnight.

Stage 3, Completed 6 September 2026

1. Introduced dual writes, with the order service writing each new order to both databases.
2. Built a reconciliation job comparing new records hourly.
3. Converted stored procedures for loyalty point calculation from MySQL syntax to PL/pgSQL.

Dual writes allowed the team to test PostgreSQL with real production traffic without depending on it. The reconciliation job found two problems in the first week: timestamps differed by seven hours because the old database stored local time without time zone information, and some product names with Vietnamese characters were truncated because the old column used a byte-limited length. Both issues were fixed before cutover. Consultant Lee Hyun-woo, who worked on a similar migration at a Korean e-commerce company, recommended the hourly reconciliation approach.

Stage 2, Completed 12 August 2026

1. Copied historical data from 2018 to 2025 using a bulk export and import pipeline.
2. Rebuilt indexes in PostgreSQL, replacing three MySQL full-text indexes with trigram indexes.
3. Partitioned the orders and order lines tables by month.

Partitioning was chosen because most queries filter by date, and it allows old partitions to be archived cheaply.

Stage 1, Completed 18 July 2026

1. Provisioned PostgreSQL 16 on the company's cloud account in the Singapore region.
2. Mapped every MySQL data type to its PostgreSQL equivalent and documented exceptions.

Next Steps

After the fallback period ends on 11 October, the MySQL instance will be decommissioned and its final backup archived for seven years under the company's data retention policy.

Alpheus C. Morse (1818-1893) was an American architect with offices in Providence, Rhode Island. Life and career Alpheus Carey Morse was born June 3, 1818, in Boston, Massachusetts to Hazen and Lucy (Cary) Morse. Hazen Morse was a noted silversmith and engraver. He was named for stonecutter Alpheus Cary, his mother's father. He was educated in architecture in the office of Alexander Parris, then one of Boston's leading architects. In 1840 he hoped to gain further experience in the office of Richard Upjohn, then engaged on Trinity Church in New York, and an associate of Parris in 1834. However, Upjohn then did not have space for an additional student. By 1842 he apparently planned to invite him to join his office, though by this time Morse had already left the country to travel abroad. Morse, in the
company of Seth Wells Cheney, traveled through Europe for five years, with a home base in Florence at the studio of Horatio Greenough. In Europe Morse devoted much time to painting and crayon portraiture. When he returned to Boston in 1847 he opened a studio on Tremont Row, where he at first continued that same work. His first architectural c
ommission was a church in Haverhill, Massachusetts, his father's native town. About 1851 Morse joined the office of English

im

migrant architect George Snell, then engaged on the design of Boston Music Hall. Morse was responsible for much of the interior decoration, and the two architects briefly formed a partnership 
after the building was completed in 1852. However, t
he firm of Snell & Morse was short-lived, and was dissolved in 1853.

In the same year, Morse was commissioned to design a house in Providence for a close friend, the artist Thomas Frederick Hoppin. This house is and was considered one of the best local examples of Italianate architecture. After that project was completed in 1855, Morse chose to remain in Providence and establish an architectural practice. He formed a partnership with architect Clifton A. Hall, but this too proved short-lived, and Morse & Hall was dissolved in 1856. For the remainder of his career Morse would be a sole practitioner. After the departure from Providence and eventual death of Thomas Alexander Tefft, Morse was the city's leading architect for several years. From 1859 to 1861 he was assisted by Alfred Stone, who himself would become a leader in the profession. Morse consistently relied on the architecture of the Italian Renaissance as a source for his own work, and was largely dedicate
d to that style. However, this fell out of favor in his later years, and he transitioned to other styles, including the High Victorian Gothic, Romanesque Revival and Queen Anne. Some of these works were innovative in the local context. Rogers Hall of Brown University, built in 1862, and the Rhode Island Hospital, built in 1864–68, were the first examples of polychrome Gothic architecture in the area, and Sayles Memorial Hall, also at Brown, was one of the area's earliest examples of Richardsonian Romanesque architecture. Personal life In 1855 Morse married Caroline Emily Pearce, daughter of Earl Douglas and Lydia (Wheaton) Pearce. The couple moved into the house at 44 Benefit Street, the southern half of a double house built in 1827 by Tallman & Bucklin for the bride's father as an investment. They lived there for the remainder of their lives, raising three daughters. Their eldest, Anne Goddard Morse, was educated as an artist in Boston and New York. In 1868, Morse was awarded an honorary Master of Arts degree from Brown
 University. The Brown professors John Larkin Lincoln and George Ide Chace were both his brothers-in-law. Morse died November 25, 1893, at home in Providence after a brief illness, at the age of 75.

Consumer Dispute Summary: Rooftop Solar Sales Practices Decision of the Saitama Consumer Affairs Center Dispute Resolution Committee, 10 September 2026, and related guidance from the Consumer Affairs Agency. Prepared for member agencies of the Kanto Consumer Advisors Network. Background of the Complaints Between 2024 and 2026, consumer centres in Saitama received 186 complaints about door-to-door sales of residential solar systems by Hidamari Energy Solutions. Most complainants were homeowners over 65 living in the suburbs of Kawagoe, Kumagaya and Higashimatsuyama. The committee selected five representative cases for its formal resolution procedure, involving contracts ranging from 2.1 million to 3.4 million yen, all financed through instalment loans arranged by the seller. Practices Identified

The committee found that sales staff had engaged in practices that included the following: * Telling homeowners that electricity savings would fully cover monthly loan repayments, based on unrealistic generation estimates * Stating that a government programme required installations to be completed by a deadline, when no such programme existed * Visiting homes repeatedly over several days and staying for more than three hours at a time
* Failing to hand over the contract document required by the Specified Commercial Transactions Act until after installation Legal Analysis

Under the Specified Commercial Transactions Act, consumers who buy through door-to-door sales may cancel within eight days of receiving a compliant contract document. Where no compliant document is delivered, the cooling-off period does not start running. The committee found that in four of the five cases the documents delivered omitted required information, including the total amount payable under the loan, so the cooling-off period had never begun. Those homeowners were therefore entitled to cancel and to have the systems removed at the seller's expense. In the fifth case, the document was compliant and the cooling-off period had expired. However, the committee found that the generation estimate presented to the homeowner assumed an optimal south-facing roof, while the actual roof faced east and was shaded by a neighbour's house for much of the afternoon. It concluded that this amounted to a misrepresentation of an important matter under the Consumer Contract Act, allowing the homeowner to rescind the contract. Outcome and Further Action Hidamari Energy Solutions agreed to cancel all five contracts and to refund payments already made, totalling 4.8 million yen. The Consumer Affairs Agency has since issued a business suspension order against the company for nine months. Advisors handling similar complaints should ask consumers for every document received, check whether the cooling-off period has started, and compare generation estimates with the roof's actual orientation and shading.

Subject: reef survey results from Watamu and what we need for the next dive season

Dear Dr Mutua,

The field team got back from Watamu Marine National Park on Sunday, and I wanted to send you the early numbers before the full report goes to the Kenya Wildlife Service. Overall the picture is mixed: some sites have recovered better than we expected after the 2024 bleaching event, while others have barely moved.

Survey Results

We ran 48 belt transects across six sites between 3 and 17 March, using the same fixed markers installed in 2021. Average live hard coral cover across all sites is now 27 percent, compared with 19 percent in the 2024 survey and 34 percent before the bleaching. Coral Garden and the outer edge of Turtle Reef did best, with Acropora tables clearly regrowing, while the lagoon sites near the Mida Creek mouth are still dominated by turf algae.

Sedimentation seems to be the main difference. Hamisi measured visibility and suspended sediment at each site and found the lagoon readings were roughly three times higher, which fits with reports of new building along the creek and the cleared mangroves near Dabaso.

What We Need

To keep the monitoring going through the October season, there are a few things I need help arranging from your side:

- Renewal of the research permit, which expires on 30 June
- Two replacement underwater slates and a spare dive computer, since one failed on the last day
- Funding for a boat for twelve days instead of eight, so we can add the Malindi sites
- A short letter of support for the local fishers' group, who want to join as observers
- Access to the county planning records for the creek developments

The fishers' involvement matters to me personally. Several of them told us that octopus catches near the lagoon have fallen sharply, and they are keen to understand whether that is connected to the reef condition. Having them on the boat would also make it much easier to explain the closed zones to the wider community.

Next Steps

I am drafting the full report now and hope to send it to you by 10 April. Amina is cleaning the photo quadrat data and will share the species counts once they have been checked against the reference collection. If you can confirm the permit renewal by mid-April, we can book the boat with Captain Salim before the holiday rates begin.

Please let me know if you would like me to present the findings at the institute seminar in May. I think the sediment story in particular would interest the coastal planning group.

With thanks, Lulu Tesfaye

There was a memorial brass to him in the quire at Old St Paul's Cathedral.

Alexander I Theopator Euergetes, surnamed Balas (), was the ruler of the Seleucid Empire from 150 BC to August 145 BC. Picked from obscurity and supported by the neighboring Roman-allied Attalid kingdom, Alexander landed in Phoenicia in 152 BC and started a civil war against Seleucid King Demetrius I Soter. Backed by mercenaries and factions of the Seleucid Empire unhappy with the existing government, he defeated Demetrius and took the crown in 150 BC. He married the princess Cleopatra Thea to seal an alliance with the neighboring Ptolemaic kingdom. His reign saw the steady retreat of the Seleucid Empire's eastern border, with important eastern satrapies such as Media being lost to the nascent Parthian Empire. In 147 BC, Demetrius II Nicator, the young son of Demetrius I, began a campaign to overthrow Balas, and civil war resumed. Alexander's ally, Ptolemaic king Ptolemy VI Philometor, moved troops into Coele-Syria to support Alexander, but then switched sides and threw his support behind Demetrius II. At the Battle of the Oenoparus River in Syria, he was defeated by Ptolemy VI and he died shortly afterward.

Life

Origins and mission to Rome
Alexander Balas claimed to be the son of Antiochus IV Epiphanes and Laodice IV and heir to the Seleucid throne. The ancient sources, Polybius and Diodorus say that this claim was false and that he and his sister Laodice VI were really natives of Smyrna of humble origin. However, Polybius became friends with Balas's rival King Demetrius I when both were hostages in Rome, so Polybius is not an unbiased source on this matter. Modern scholars disagree about whether the story of Attalus finding a commoner who looked the part is true or was propaganda put about by Alexander's opponents.

According to Diodorus, Alexander was originally put forward as a candidate for the Seleucid throne by Attalus II of Pergamum. Attalus had been disturbed by the Seleucid king Demetrius I's interference in Cappadocia, where he had dethroned king Ariarathes V. Boris Chrubasik is sceptical, noting that there is little subsequent evidence for Attalid involvement with Alexander. However, Selene Psoma has proposed that a large set of coins minted in a number of cities under Attalid control in this period was produced by Attalus II in order to fund Alexander's bid for the kingship.

Alexander and his sister were maintained in Cilicia by Heracleides, a former minister of Antiochus IV and brother of Timarchus, an usurper in Media who had been executed by the reigning king Demetrius I Soter. In 153 BC, Heracleides brought Alexander and his sister to Rome, where he presented Alexander to the Roman Senate, which recognised him as the legitimate Seleucid king and agreed to support him in his bid to take the throne. Polybius mentions that Attalus II and Demetrius I also met with the Senate at this time but does not state how this was connected to the recognition of Alexander - if at all.

War with Demetrius I (152–150 BC)

After recruiting mercenaries, Alexander and Heracleides departed to Ephesus. From there, they invaded Phoenicia by sea, seizing Ptolemais Akko. Numismatic evidence shows that Alexander had also gained control of Seleucia Pieria, Byblos, Beirut, Tyre by 151 BC. On this coinage, Alexander heavily advertised his (claimed) connection to Antiochus IV, depicting Zeus Nicephorus on his coinage as Antiochus had done. He also assumed the title of Theopator ('Divinely Fathered'), which recalled Antiochus' epithet Theos Epiphanes ('God Manifest'). The coinage also presented Alexander Balas in the guise of Alexander the Great, with pronounced facial features and long flowing hair. This was intended to emphasise his military prowess to his soldiers.

WheelWright Workshop Software, release history for the 2026 builds used by independent bike shops in Australia and New Zealand

Most of our customers are two or three person workshops who book repairs on paper until things get busy, then switch to WheelWright to stop jobs falling through the cracks. The notes below explain each change in plain terms, because several shop owners told us the old release notes read like they were written for programmers.

Release 7.4, 11 September 2026

* Added a parts-on-order status for jobs, so a bike waiting for a Shimano rear derailleur no longer shows as overdue and clogs the dashboard
* Customer SMS now includes an estimated pick-up time window rather than a single time, after shops in Geelong and Newcastle said customers arrived too early and waited in the store
* Fixed a bug where splitting a service into two invoices dropped the labour line from the second invoice
* The tyre size lookup now recognises 29 by 2.6 inch and 700 by 45c sizes common on gravel bikes

The parts-on-order status is the change most shops asked about. Previously a job had only three states, which meant a bike sitting in the back room for a week waiting for parts looked identical to a bike that a mechanic had forgotten about. Owners now see waiting jobs in a separate grey column and can filter them out when planning the day.

Release 7.3, 24 July 2026

This release concentrated on the service menu. Shops can now create bundled services, such as a Gold Service that includes a chain, cassette and brake pad replacement, and set a single price that adjusts automatically when parts prices change. Bundles were requested by Pedal Republic in Fremantle, whose staff were manually adding the same eight line items to every major service.

We also removed the old print layout for job tickets. Fewer than two percent of shops were still using it, and keeping it working was delaying other fixes.

Release 7.2, 5 June 2026

Stock counts now sync with Lightspeed every fifteen minutes instead of hourly. Faster syncing matters most on Saturday mornings, when a busy shop can sell its last inner tube of a given size at the counter while a mechanic is quoting that same tube on a repair.

Looking Ahead

Version 7.5 is planned for late October and will add e-bike battery health recording, with fields for cycle count and the diagnostic reading from Bosch and Shimano tools. Send feature requests to Tamsin Galloway at support@wheelwright.net.au.

Kumasi Repair Shops Struggle to Keep Up as City Turns to Bicycles

The narrow workshop of Kwame Adjei on the edge of Kejetia market has never been so busy. Eight bicycles lean against the wall waiting for attention, and two apprentices are tru
ing wheels on a bench made from an old door. "Three years ago I fixed maybe ten bicycles a week," Adjei said on Wednesday, wiping grease from his hands. "Now I turn customers away every afternoon." Fuel prices and traffic are the main reasons. Since petrol passed GHS 15 per litre in 2026, a growing number of Kumasi residents have abandoned taxis and okadas for short journeys. The Kumasi Metropolitan Assembly estimates that bicycle trips in the central business district rose by about 60

 percent between 2025 and 2027, helped by a painted cycle lane along Harper Road and the new bike racks at Kumasi Central Market. A Shortage of Parts and Skills Mechanics interviewed for this article described the same set of problems: • Spare parts arrive irregularly from Tema port, and inner tubes in common sizes sometimes run out for two weeks at a time. • Cheap imported bicycles break more often, especially their bottom brackets and plastic pedals. • Few young people want to train as mechanics because the pay is low and the work is dirty. • Many customers wait until a fault is serious instead of coming in for basic servicing. Adjei charges GHS 25 to fix a puncture and GHS 120 for a full service that includes cleaning and adjusting the gears and brakes. He says many riders cannot afford the full service and keep riding with worn brake pads, which he considers dangerous on the steep roads near Bantama.

Training Efforts The Ashanti Regional office of the Council for Technical and Vocational Education and Training began 
a six-month bicycle mechanics course at the Kumasi Technical Institute in January. The first group of 24 trainees, including seven young women, will finish in July. Course coordinator Mrs Akosua Owusu-Ansah said the curriculum covers wheel building, gear systems, brake maintenance and running a small business, and that every trainee will spend the final two months attached to an established workshop.

Adjei has agreed to take two trainees. "If they are serious, I will teach them everything," he said. "There is enough work for all of us now." Calls for Support

The Kumasi Cycling Association has asked the metropolitan assembly to reduce the daily market toll for roadside repairers and to set aside space for a cluster of workshops near the planned bus terminal at Adum. An assembly spokesperson said the request would be considered as part of the 2028 budget discussions.

2 Related Work and Research Gap Maintenance planning for onshore wind turbines has been studied from three main perspectives: reliability engineering, which focuses on failure rates of individual components; operations research, which optimises the scheduling of repair crews and vessels; and data-driven condition monitoring, which aims to predict failures from sensor signals.
 Our study, which examines maintenance practice on small wind farms in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, draws on all three strands but addresses a context they ha
ve largely overlooked. 2.1 Reliability Studies Large reliability databases such as those compiled in Germany and Sweden have established that gearboxes, generators and blades ca
use the longest downtimes, while electrical and control syst
ems fail most often. These studies, however, draw almost entirely on turbines owned by large utilities with in-house maintenance teams and full-service contracts. Turbines in Central Europe are frequently owned by small investors or municipal companies with only a handful of machines, often of older or di
scontinued models, and the extent to which the established failure patterns apply to them is unknown. 2.2 Scheduling
and Logistics Operations research on maintenance scheduling has concentrated mostly on offshore wind, where access is limited by wave
 height and vessel availability. Onshore studies are fewer and usually assume that cranes and spare parts are available
on demand. Interviews conducted by Kubica and Slováková in 2024 with operators in the
 Ore Mountains co
ntradicted this assumption, report
ing crane waiting times of several months for main component replacements. 2.3 Condition Monitoring
The literature on condition monitoring has grown quickly with the availability of SCADA data and machine learning 
methods. Reported results are often impressive but are based on large fleets of identical turbines, which provide enough failure examples to train models. Small owners with mixed fleets rarely have such data. 2.4 Identified Gap Taken together, previous work leaves several questions open for the small-fleet context that dominates our region:
•
 Whether failure rates and downtime distributions match those reported from large utility fleets. • How much of total downtime
 is caused by logistics rather
than by the repair itself

2 Related Work and Research Gap

Maintenance planning for onshore wind turbines has been studied from three main perspectives: reliability engineering, which focuses on failure rates of individual components; operations research, which optimises the scheduling of repair crews and vessels; and data-driven condition monitoring, which aims to predict failures from sensor signals. Our study, which examines maintenance practice on small wind farms in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, draws on all three strands but addresses a context they have largely overlooked.

2.1 Reliability Studies

Large reliability databases such as those compiled in Germany and Sweden have established that gearboxes, generators and blades cause the longest downtimes, while electrical and control systems fail most often. These studies, however, draw almost entirely on turbines owned by large utilities with in-house maintenance teams and full-service contracts. Turbines in Central Europe are frequently owned by small investors or municipal companies with only a handful of machines, often of older or discontinued models, and the extent to which the established failure patterns apply to them is unknown.

2.2 Scheduling and Logistics

Operations research on maintenance scheduling has concentrated mostly on offshore wind, where access is limited by wave height and vessel availability. Onshore studies are fewer and usually assume that cranes and spare parts are available on demand. Interviews conducted by Kubica and Slováková in 2024 with operators in the Ore Mountains contradicted this assumption, reporting crane waiting times of several months for main component replacements.

2.3 Condition Monitoring

The literature on condition monitoring has grown quickly with the availability of SCADA data and machine learning methods. Reported results are often impressive but are based on large fleets of identical turbines, which provide enough failure examples to train models. Small owners with mixed fleets rarely have such data.

2.4 Identified Gap

Taken together, previous work leaves several questions open for the small-fleet context that dominates our region:

• Whether failure rates and downtime distributions match those reported from large utility fleets.
• How much of total downtime is caused by logistics rather than by the repair itself.
• Whether owners of fewer than five turbines can realistically benefit from condition monitoring.
• How maintenance contracts with manufacturers or independent service providers affect availability.

Our study addresses these questions using maintenance records from 23 turbines owned by eight operators, complemented by interviews with owners and service technicians. Section 3 describes the data and the interview protocol in detail.

Gumbo soil is a mixtur
e which often has some small amounts of sand and/or organic material, but is typically defined by the overwhelming presence of very fine particles of clay. Although gumbo soils are exceptional at water retention, they can be difficult to farm, as precipitation will turn gumbo into a unique muddy mess that is challenging to work using large commercial farming equipment. Avoiding tillage of this type of soil through no-till farming appears strongly correlated with higher yields, as compared to more traditional tilling practices.

Release History: Fiskeappen for iOS and Android

Fiskeappen helps anglers in Norway and Sweden find fishing spots, buy fishing licences and log catches. It is developed by a four-person team at Fiskeappen AS in Kristiansand. This page lists recent releases with notes explaining the reasoning behind each change, written mainly for our support staff and for users who like to know why things work the way they do.

Version 5.4, 30 September 2026

1. Licence purchase now supports more than 1,200 Swedish waters through integration with iFiske.
2. Catch logs can be exported as a CSV file for personal records or club competitions.
3. Offline maps are compressed more efficiently and take up about 35 percent less storage.
4. Fixed a crash when adding a photo to a catch log on some older Samsung phones.

Swedish licence support was the most requested feature among users in Värmland and Dalsland, who often fish on both sides of the border and previously had to switch between apps. The export feature was requested by fishing clubs that run catch-and-release competitions and needed a simple way to collect results. Offline map compression matters because many popular fishing areas in the mountains have no mobile coverage, and some users with older phones were running out of storage.

Version 5.3, 26 August 2026

1. Added water temperature and water level data for 340 rivers from the Norwegian Water Resources and Energy Directorate.
2. Introduced a reminder to report salmon catches before the end of the season.
3. Changed the default map view to satellite imagery in mountain areas.

Water level data helps salmon and trout anglers decide when and where to fish, since conditions in rivers like the Gaula and Namsen can change dramatically after rain. The reporting reminder was added at the request of several river owner associations, who rely on catch reports to manage salmon stocks and set quotas.

Version 5.2, 15 July 2026

1. Users can now mark spots as private, so they are never shown to other anglers.
2. Improved accuracy of sunrise and sunset times in northern Norway.

Some users were worried that their favourite spots would become crowded if shared with others, even unintentionally. Private spots are stored only on the user's device unless they choose to sync them to their own account. The sunrise fix addresses a calculation error that made times inaccurate by up to 20 minutes north of the Arctic Circle during midnight sun periods.

Coming Next

Version 5.5 is planned for November and will add tide tables for coastal fishing, a feature many sea anglers in Western Norway have asked for.

Moisture Damage in
Renovated Kitchens: Inspection Results from 48 Swedish Homes Technical report prepared by Fuktcentrum Väst AB for the insurance company Länsförsäkringar Älvsborg. Authors: Susanne Ljung and Tobias Hermansson. Reference FV-2026-118, dated 22 September 2026.
 1 Introduction

Water damage in kitchens is one of the most frequent and costly types of insurance claims in Swedish homes. Länsförsäkringar Älvsborg noticed that a significant share of kitchen water damage claims came from kitchens renovated within the previous five years. The insurer commissioned this study to 
identify common construction and installation errors and to propose guidance for homeowners and contractors. 2 Method Between February and July 2026 we inspected 48 homes in Borås, Alingsås and Vänersborg where a kitchen renovated between 2019 and 2024 had been the source of an insurance claim. Each inspection included a visual examination, moisture measurements in floors and walls, thermal imaging and, where possible, interviews with the homeowner and documentation from the contractor. 3 Main Findings The most common causes of damage, in order of frequency, were: 1. Leaks from dishwasher connections, usually because the inlet hose had been kinked or the connection overtightened. 2. Missing or incorrectly installed drip trays under dishwashe
rs and sinks, so that leaks spread unnoticed under cabinets.
3. Poorly sealed joints between the worktop and the sink or hob, allowing water to penetrate the worktop core.
4. Refrigerators with ice makers connected to the water supply by inexperienced installers without a shut-off valve.
5. Condensation behind cabinets mounted directly against cold external walls. In 29 of the 48 homes, the leak had continued for weeks or months before being discovered, causing mould growth in the floor structure. Drip trays with leak sensors were present in only five of the homes, and none of those suffered e
xtensive damage.

4 Discussion Many renovations were carried out by contractors who were not certified under the Säker Vatten industry rules, which set requirements for kitchen and bathroom installations. In several cases, homeowners had installed appliances themselves after the contractor finished the cabinets. Damage was especially severe in homes with wooden floor structures, where moisture spread easily. The findings suggest that relatively simple measures could prevent most of the damage. A drip tray with a leak sensor costs around SEK 400 and can be installed in minutes, while repairing a damaged kitchen floor often costs SEK 150,000 or more. 5 Recommendations We recommend that the insurer encourage policyholders to use certified contractors, offer reduced deductibles for kitchens with le
ak sensors and automatic shut-off valves, and publish a short checklist for homeowners planning a renovation. Contractors should document each water connection with photographs before cabinets are closed.

Moisture Damage in Renovated Kitchens: Inspection Results from 48 Swedish Homes

Technical report prepared by Fuktcentrum Väst AB for the insurance company Länsförsäkringar Älvsborg. Authors: Susanne Ljung and Tobias Hermansson. Reference FV-2026-118, dated 22 September 2026.

1 Introduction

Water damage in kitchens is one of the most frequent and costly types of insurance claims in Swedish homes. Länsförsäkringar Älvsborg noticed that a significant share of kitchen water damage claims came from kitchens renovated within the previous five years. The insurer commissioned this study to identify common construction and installation errors and to propose guidance for homeowners and contractors.

2 Method

Between February and July 2026 we inspected 48 homes in Borås, Alingsås and Vänersborg where a kitchen renovated between 2019 and 2024 had been the source of an insurance claim. Each inspection included a visual examination, moisture measurements in floors and walls, thermal imaging and, where possible, interviews with the homeowner and documentation from the contractor.

3 Main Findings

The most common causes of damage, in order of frequency, were:

1. Leaks from dishwasher connections, usually because the inlet hose had been kinked or the connection overtightened.
2. Missing or incorrectly installed drip trays under dishwashers and sinks, so that leaks spread unnoticed under cabinets.
3. Poorly sealed joints between the worktop and the sink or hob, allowing water to penetrate the worktop core.
4. Refrigerators with ice makers connected to the water supply by inexperienced installers without a shut-off valve.
5. Condensation behind cabinets mounted directly against cold external walls.

In 29 of the 48 homes, the leak had continued for weeks or months before being discovered, causing mould growth in the floor structure. Drip trays with leak sensors were present in only five of the homes, and none of those suffered extensive damage.

4 Discussion

Many renovations were carried out by contractors who were not certified under the Säker Vatten industry rules, which set requirements for kitchen and bathroom installations. In several cases, homeowners had installed appliances themselves after the contractor finished the cabinets. Damage was especially severe in homes with wooden floor structures, where moisture spread easily.

The findings suggest that relatively simple measures could prevent most of the damage. A drip tray with a leak sensor costs around SEK 400 and can be installed in minutes, while repairing a damaged kitchen floor often costs SEK 150,000 or more.

5 Recommendations

We recommend that the insurer encourage policyholders to use certified contractors, offer reduced deductibles for kitchens with leak sensors and automatic shut-off valves, and publish a short checklist for homeowners planning a renovation. Contractors should document each water connection with photographs before cabinets are closed.

Funding Application: Integrated Bus and Rail Timetabling for the Hawke's
Bay Region Submitted to the Waka Kotahi NZ Transport Agency Innovation Fund by Hawke's Bay Regional Council, in partnership with Napier City Council, Hastings District Council and KiwiRail. Applicant contact: Joseph Wharerau, Transport Planning Manager. Requested funding: 485,000 dollars over 24 months. Summary Hawke's Bay currently has no passenger rail service, but a feasibility study published in 2025 recommended trialling a weekday commuter service between Napier and Hastings using existing freight lines. If that
 trial proceeds, its success will depend heavily on how well trains connect with the region's goBay bus network. This project would develop an integrated timetable that coordinates bus and rail services from the start, rather than trying to match them after the fact. The Problem Across New Zealand, regional rail services

 have often been introduced with timetables designed in isolation from local buses. Passengers arriving by train then face long waits for connecting buses, or miss them e
ntirely, which discourages people from switching from cars. Hawke's Bay has an opportunity to avoid this mistake by planning both networks together before any train runs. Project Activities Over two years, the project would deliver several connected pieces of work:

* A travel survey of 2,500 households in Napi
er, Hastings, Havelock North and Clive to understand current commuting patterns * Modelling of potential train paths on the Palmerston North to Gisborne line, taking freight movements into account * Development of three integrated timetable options, with bus routes adjusted to meet trains at Napier, Hastings and a proposed new stop at Whakatū * Community consultation on the options, including hui with Ngāti Kahungunu and engagement with major employers such as Napier Port and Hawke's Bay Hospital * A final recommended 
timetable and implementation plan for both networks Why This Approach Matters Integrated timetabling is standard practice in Switzerland, the Netherlands and parts of Germany, where trains and buses are scheduled together so transfers take only a few minutes. A successful project here would provide a model for other regions considering new rail services, such as Waikato's extension of Te Huia and proposed services in Canterbury. Budget

its existing bus network
 monitoring.

Expected Outcomes At the end of the project, the region will have a fully integrated bus and rail timetable ready to implement if the rail trial is approved. We will publish all survey data
, modelling methods and lessons learned so that other councils can benefit from the work.

PaceForge Coach: Marathon Plan Builder Product documentation, version 4.2, PaceForge Labs, Waterloo, Ontario

PaceForge Coach generates personalised marathon training plans for recreational runners and adjusts them each week based on completed workouts. Running clubs, physiotherapy clinics and individual coaches use it to manage groups of athlet
es from a single dashboard. This page explains how the plan builder works, which inputs it requires and how its weekly adjustments are calculated. It is written for coaches and club administrators rather than for individual runners. Inputs Required

To create a plan, the coach or runner enters basic informati
on that the builder uses to set training zones and weekly volume. The plan is only as good as these inputs, so encourage athletes to be honest about their current fitness rather than their hopes. The builder asks for the following: 1. A recent ra
ce result, ideally a half marathon or 10 km from the last three months. 2. Current average weekly distance over the previous four weeks. 3. The date of the target marathon and a goal time, which is optional. 4. Days of the week available for 
running, and which day suits the long run. 5. Any injuries in the last year, selected from a list of common running injuries.

How the Plan Is Built The builder estimates the runner's current thres
hold pace from the race result using a modified Daniels formula. It then chooses a plan length between twelve and twenty weeks depending on the time remaining before the race and on the gap between
 current and recommended vol
ume. Weekly distance increases by no more than 10 percent, and every fourth week is a recove
ry week at about 75 percent of the previous week's volume. The longest run is capped at 32 km or three and a half hours, whichever comes first. Weekly Adjustments Each Monday, PaceForge compares the past week's completed workouts, imported from Garmin, Coros, Polar or Strava, with the planned workouts. If the runner completed less than 70 percent of planned volu
me, the following week is reduced rather than increased. If heart rate during easy runs is consistently higher than expected for the pace, the builder flags possible fatigue or illness and notifies the coach.
 Coaches can override any adjustment. Group Features Clubs such as the Kitchener-Waterloo Road Runners use 
the group dashboard to see all members' plans at once. The dashboard highlights runners who have missed several sessions, those whose plans have been reduced twice in a row, and those approaching race day. Coaches can send a message to a whole pace group from the dashboard. Limitations PaceForge is not a medical device and cannot diagnose injuries. Its pace estimates are less reliable for runners whose only recent result is a short race, such as a 5 km,
 or a race run in extreme heat. For support, contact help@paceforge.ca or our office at 151 Charles Street West, Kitchener.

Beth Ann Arnoult-Ritthaler (born December 1, 1965) is a retired American wheelchair tennis player who competed in international level events. She was a silver medalist at the 2007 Parapan American Games. She was a quarterfinalist in the women's singles in the 2008 Summer Paralympics and was fourth place in the women's doubles with Kaitlyn Verfuerth.

Arnoult was paralysed from a car accident with an all-terrain vehicle in 1991 when her vertebrae were shattered leaving her paralysed.

Saulė Mount SR-40 Roof Rail System: Installation Guide for Pitched Tile Roofs Applies to kit versions SR-40A and SR-40B, sold in Lithuania, Latvia and Poland
 from January 2026. Manufactured by Saulės Konstrukcijos UAB, Panevėžys. Before You Start This guide covers mounting framed photovoltaic modules on pitched roofs covered with clay or concrete tiles, at angles from 15 to 60 degrees. The SR-40 system is designed for modules between 1,650 and 2,280 millimetres long, weighing up to 32 kilograms each. Installation must be carried out
by a qualified installer, and electrical connection
must be made by a licensed electrician in accordance with national regulations. Check the snow and wind load zone for the building's location; in zone III and above, which includes much of the Baltic coast, roof hooks must be spaced no more than 1,000 millimetres apart. Contents of the Kit Each standard kit for a row of four modules contains:

- Eight adjustable stainless steel roof hooks with M8 fixing bolts. - Two aluminium rails, 4,400 millimetres long, with a pre-drilled splice plate.
- Six mid clamps and
four end clamps sized for module frames of 30 to 40 millimetres. - Earthing clips and a bonding jumper for the rail splice.
- Hammerhead bolts and flange nuts, with ten percent spares.

Installation Steps Begin by marking the module field on the roof, leaving at least 500 millimetres free from the ridge 
and from each edge. Remove the tiles where the hooks will be placed and fix each hook to a rafter with two 8 by 100 millimetre wood screws, never to the battens alone. Adjust the hook height so that it sits in the valley of the tile below without lifting it. Grind a small notch in the underside of t
he upper tile if needed, then replace the tiles and check that they lie flat and do not rock. Fasten the rails to the hooks using the hammerhead bolts, tightening to 15 newton metres. Use a string line to make sure both rails

are straight and parallel; misalignment of more than 5 millimetres over the rail length will make clamping difficult. Join rails with the splice plate and fit the bonding jumper across the joint.

Place the first module on the rails and secure it with two end
 clamps. Fit mid clamps between modules and tighten all clamps to 12 newton metres. Leave the protective film on the module glass until all mechanical work is finished.

Inspection and Warranty After installation, inspect the roof from inside the loft to make sure no screws have missed the rafters. Record hook positions and torque values on the commissioning form supplied with the kit. The SR-40 system carries a fifteen-year warranty against corrosion and structural failure when installed according to this guide. The warranty does not
 cover damage caused by fixing hooks to battens, using non-original fasteners, or exceeding the stated load zones. For technical support, contact the Saulės Konstrukcijos hotline on weekdays bet
ween 8:00 and 17:00.

Coaching career

After graduating from university, he began working at 1.FC Eschborn as a chief scout. Two years later, he became the team's assistant coach and was promoted as the team manager in 2001, a post he kept until 2004. In July 2005, he was appointed as the manager of KSV Baunatal but was sacked at the end of the season. After Afshin Ghotbi appointed as head coach of Persepolis, he was named as one of his assistants, alongside he worked as fitness trainer at the club. After resignation of Ghotbi, he left the team to become DAC Dunajská Streda's assistant coach. He also works with Hamid Estili as his assistant in Steel Azin. He was Montenegro national football team's assistant to Zlatko Kranjčar from 2009 until 2010. After Kranjčar became head coach of Sepahan in November 2011, he was named as his first team coach. He left the team after a series of problems with the management in December 2012. He has worked in IRIB's Varzesh channel as a football analyst. On 15 August 2013, he became assistant coach of Akbar Misaghian at Azadegan League side Padideh Shandiz. After Misaghian resigned despite promoting Padideh to the Iran Pro League, Marzban was named as his successor.

Interior Construction Technology, Lecture 11: Kitchen Renovation in Historic Buildings

Slovak University of Technology in Bratislava, Faculty of Architecture and Design. Lecturer: Ing. arch. Monika Šuleková, PhD. Notes prepared by the course assistant for students who missed the session on 26 November.

Introduction

Last week we dealt with kitchens in prefabricated panel flats, where the main constraints were the concrete walls and the installation core. Historic town houses present a completely different set of problems. The case study today is a second-floor flat in a listed burgher house on Hlavná street in Levoča, built in the sixteenth century and remodelled around 1880, where the owners wanted to convert a former maid's room into an open kitchen connected to the living room.

Heritage Constraints

Any change in a listed building needs a binding opinion from the regional monuments board, in this case the Prešov office. The board's conservator visited the flat with the architect before any design work began. Students should remember that the board cares about historically valuable elements, not about modern finishes, so the conversation goes better if you arrive with a survey that separates the two.

In the Levoča flat the survey found a vaulted ceiling with remains of painted decoration, original plank floors under a later layer of linoleum, and a chimney flue that once served a tiled stove. Each of these shaped the design.

Design Decisions

The architect and the owners agreed on the following approach, which the board approved with minor conditions:

1. Keep the vaulted ceiling exposed and free of any fixings, with lighting on freestanding rails along the walls.
2. Restore the plank floor in the living area but lay a new tiled floor in the kitchen zone on a separating membrane that can be removed later.
3. Run new water and waste pipes in a raised plinth behind the units rather than chasing them into the historic walls.
4. Use the old flue for the extractor duct after a camera inspection confirmed it was sound.
5. Choose freestanding kitchen furniture that does not need to be fixed to the vaulted wall.

Moisture and Ventilation

Thick stone walls in historic buildings breathe, and covering them with impermeable tiles or vinyl wallpaper can trap moisture and cause plaster to fail. A lime-based plaster and mineral paint were used instead of a full tiled splashback, with a glass panel only directly behind the hob.

Costs and Time

The Levoča project took eleven months from survey to completion, of which four months were spent waiting for the board's opinion and a restorer's report on the ceiling. The construction cost of 41,000 EUR was roughly 30 percent higher than a comparable kitchen in a modern flat. Seminar groups should compare this with the panel flat budget from Lecture 10 and identify which cost items differ most.

3 Data and Methods

3.1 Setting

The study draws on applicant tracking data from a mid-sized Korean electronics components firm with manufacturing and engineering sites in Gumi, Korea, and in Thai Nguyen and Bac Giang provinces, Vietnam. In March 2024 the firm replaced its unstructured interview process for engineering and supervisory roles with a structured process consisting of a standardised screening rubric, a work sample test and a panel interview with fixed questions and anchored rating scales. The change was introduced at all sites on the same date, but implementation quality varied, which provides useful variation for analysis.

3.2 Sample

Our sample covers all 6,218 applications for engineering and supervisory positions received between January 2022 and December 2025, of which 2,741 arrived before the change and 3,477 after. For each application, the firm's human resources analytics team, led by Ms. Bang Eun-sol, supplied de-identified records including the stage reached, interviewer ratings, final decision, and, for those hired, performance ratings and retention status at twelve months. Applicant gender, age band, university tier and nationality were recorded, but names and contact details were removed before transfer.

3.3 Outcome Measures

We examine four outcomes, chosen to capture both efficiency and fairness of hiring:

* Time to decision, measured in calendar days from application to offer or rejection.
* Inter-rater reliability of interview scores, measured by the intraclass correlation among panel members.
* Gaps in offer rates between applicant groups defined by gender and university tier.
* Twelve-month performance ratings and retention among hired candidates.

3.4 Identification Strategy

Because the change was introduced everywhere at once, a simple before-and-after comparison would confound the new process with other changes over time, such as labour market conditions after the pandemic. We therefore exploit variation in implementation fidelity. Using audit records, we classify each hiring panel after March 2024 as high-fidelity if it used all structured elements in at least 90 percent of interviews and low-fidelity otherwise. Fidelity was notably lower at the newest site in Bac Giang, where several managers had joined from firms with very different hiring cultures, according to site HR manager Mr. Duong Van Thanh. We then estimate difference-in-differences models comparing changes in outcomes between panels that later became high-fidelity and those that remained low-fidelity, controlling for site, role and year.

3.5 Limitations

Panels were not randomly assigned to fidelity levels, and managers who embraced structured interviewing may differ in other ways, such as being more experienced. We address this partly by controlling for manager tenure and by checking whether pre-change trends differed across the two groups, which they did not appear to. Performance ratings are themselves subjective and may reflect the same biases that structured interviews aim to reduce, so we treat the performance outcome with caution. Finally, results from one firm may not generalise to industries with different hiring practices.

Smiukampen is a mountain in Sel Municipality in Innlandet county, Norway. The tall mountain is located in the Rondane mountains within Rondane National Park. The mountain sits about northeast of the town of Otta. The mountain is surrounded by several other notable mountains including Bråkdalsbelgen, Sagtindan, and Indre Bråkdalshøe to the northwest; and Ljosåbelgen, Hoggbeitet, and Smiubelgen to the northeast.

Renovating the Communal Kitchen at Tumaini Children's Home, Kisii A funding request to the Gusii Development Trust Small Grants Programme. Applicant: Tumaini Children's Home, Nyanchwa, Kisii town. Amount requested: KSh 1,480,000.

Tumaini Children's
Home cares for 46 children aged between three and seventee

n, most of whom were referred by the Kisii children's office after losing one or both pa
rents. Three meals a day are prepared in a kitchen built in 1998, which has never been renovated. Last month the county public health officer gave us ninety days to fix serious hygiene and safety problems or face closure of the kitchen, which would force us to buy cooked food at a cost we cannot sustain. Current Condition The kitchen measures roughly six by four metres and is used by two cooks, Mama Kerubo Nyaboke and Mama Moraa Ondieki, who have worked here for over ten years. Food is cooked on three open wood fires, which fill the room with smoke and have caused repeated eye and chest complaints. The floor is cracked earth covered with old cement, impossible to clean properly, and the only water point is a tap outside the building. The roof leaks in four places during the long rains, and the single window does not o
pen. Proposed Works We have obtained a quotation from a local contractor approved by the Kisii county works department. The renovation would include: • Two energy-saving institutional jikos with chimneys, replacing the open fires • A new concrete floor with a smooth screed finish and a floor drain • An indoor stainless steel sink with piped water from the existing tank • Replacement of the roof sheets and gutters over the kitchen • Two new opening windows with insect mesh for ventilation
• Washable wall tiles to a height of 1.5 metres around the cooking area

Expected Benefits The energy-saving stoves alone should reduce firewood use by around 60 percent, saving the home approximately KSh 9,000 a month, which will be redirected to buying fresh vegetables and milk. Removing smoke from the room will protect the cooks' health and allow older children to help with meal preparation as part of their life skills programme without being exposed to harmful fumes. Above all, meeting the public health standards will keep the kitchen open. Timeline and Management Work would take about five weeks and can be completed during the August school holidays, when meals can be prepared temporarily under a tent with borrowed gas burners. The home's management committee, chaired by retired head teacher Mr Charles Nyamweya, will oversee payments, which will be released in three stages after inspection by a volunteer engineer from Kisii University. We have attached the contractor's quotation, the public health notice, our audited accounts for 2025 and photographs of the current kitchen. We would be grateful for
a visit from the Trust's officers at any convenient time.

The floor is cracked earth covered with old cement, impossible to clean properly, and the only water point is a tap outside the building. The roof leaks in four places during the long rains, and the single window does not open.

Proposed Works

We have obtained a quotation from a local contractor approved by the Kisii county works department. The renovation would include:

• Two energy-saving institutional jikos with chimneys, replacing the open fires
• A new concrete floor with a smooth screed finish and a floor drain
• An indoor stainless steel sink with piped water from the existing tank
• Replacement of the roof sheets and gutters over the kitchen
• Two new opening windows with insect mesh for ventilation
• Washable wall tiles to a height of 1.5 metres around the cooking area

Expected Benefits

The energy-saving stoves alone should reduce firewood use by around 60 percent, saving the home approximately KSh 9,000 a month, which will be redirected to buying fresh vegetables and milk. Removing smoke from the room will protect the cooks' health and allow older children to help with meal preparation as part of their life skills programme without being exposed to harmful fumes. Above all, meeting the public health standards will keep the kitchen open.

Timeline and Management

Work would take about five weeks and can be completed during the August school holidays, when meals can be prepared temporarily under a tent with borrowed gas burners. The home's management committee, chaired by retired head teacher Mr Charles Nyamweya, will oversee payments, which will be released in three stages after inspection by a volunteer engineer from Kisii University.

We have attached the contractor's quotation, the public health notice, our audited accounts for 2025 and photographs of the current kitchen. We would be grateful for a visit from the Trust's officers at any convenient time.

Clara Perra (Naples November 1954 - Roseto degli Abruzzi - August 2015) was an Italian solo percussionist , music educator, pianist and composer. She was the first Italian woman to hold concerts of percussion instruments and to teach them in State conservatories. Author of compositions and educational works, Clara Perra won several national auditions and an international competition, at the Orchestra of the Teatro di San Carlo in Naples. She played at the Italy on Stage festival in New York and in several concert tours she performed in repertoires ranging from classics transcribed for vibraphone, like Schumann, Bach and Mozart to the "classics" of contemporary music such as Varese and Cage (which, among other things, included the percus
sion part and the prepared piano of "Amores" performed for the first time ever in Naples). Biography Early life Despite having started to study piano at the age of six, she did 

not expect to pursue a career in music until much later in life. After listening to a concert of percussion instruments as a young adult, she “succumbed” to the "rataplan" rhythms,
an event that convinced her to leave medical school and enrol in the music conservatory.
In a short time, she graduated in piano and percussion instruments (the latter degree with honours and a special academic mention) and began studying composition with Aladino Di Martino, director of the "San Pietro a Majella " Conservatory in Naples. Career In 1984 she was the only Italian percussionist to become part of the Orchestre des Jeunes de la Mediterranee (with which she performed in major European capitals). Later, she won four national auditions and an international competition at the Orchestra
of the Teatro di San Carlo in Naples. She played in this theatre for over a decade, collaborating with world renowned conductors and performers. She was recognised and praised for both her work
as a percussionist and as a conductor, and had

to overcome some cultural bias against women playing percussion instruments.

She played at the Italy on stage festival in New York (1987); at the Wiesbaden festival (1983) and seve
ral International Festivals of Ravello; she directed various groups of 
percussionists and participated in numerous recordings of contemporary and experimental music. Before completing her musical studies, she was already part of the Franco Ferrara Orchestra, the Scarlatti RAI, the jazz-symphonic Italian Symphony Orchestra and the soloists of the Tempo
di Percussione Ensemble, a formation with which she also performed during the concert season at the Teatro di San Carlo. Regarding her teaching material, she illustrated the technique contained in the DVD "Percussion and Drums School" (Curci 1
995);
 she participated in the recording of the CD accompanying the book "Beyond the Rudiments" (Carisch 2004); she wrote essays, compositions and methods. Particular highlights include the work released in two volumes "Music Between Rhythm and Creativity" (Curci 1987): a project in collaboration with Antonio Buonomo, for which the newspaper "Corriere della Sera" devoted a full page review) and "Il Braccio del Tempo" (Simeoli 2015): a handbook that reveals the "secrets" of the orchestra pi
t, with amusing anecdotes about the conductors. It clarifies the concept of "visual rhythm" and concludes with polyrhythm exercises for two and three voices.

Oaxaca's Pan de Yema Bakers Win Protected Status After Decade-Long Campaign

Bakers in the Valles Centrales of Oaxaca celebrated on Monday after Mexico's Institute of Industrial Property granted a collective trademark to pan de yema produced by traditional methods in eight municipalities, a recognition they had sought since 2016.

The rich egg-yolk bread, often dipped in hot chocolate, is a fixture at breakfasts, weddings and the Day of the Dead altars that families build each November. Producers say industrial bakeries in Puebla and Mexico City have sold imitations under the same name for years, often made with colourants instead of fresh yolks and baked in electric ovens rather than wood-fired ones.

What the Trademark Requires

To use the new collective mark, bakers must belong to the Unión de Panaderos Tradicionales de los Valles Centrales and follow a set of production rules approved by the institute. Representatives of the union outlined the main conditions at a press conference in Santa María del Tule:

1. Dough must contain at least twelve fresh egg yolks per kilogram of flour.
2. Bread must rise naturally for at least four hours before baking.
3. Loaves must be baked in wood-fired brick ovens using local firewood or mesquite.
4. Each bakery must be located in one of the eight registered municipalities.
5. Producers must accept two unannounced inspections per year.

Who Benefits

The union counts 214 member bakeries, most of them family businesses with fewer than five workers. Its president, Fortino Hernández Cruz, whose family has baked in San Antonino Castillo Velasco for four generations, said that buyers in Oaxaca city are willing to pay more for authentic bread, but until now they had no way of telling it apart. He hopes that the mark will allow members to sell to restaurants and shops in other states at fair prices.

Not all bakers are pleased. Some smaller producers in the Mixteca region, outside the eight municipalities, say they also make the bread traditionally and have been excluded. Margarita Santiago López, who runs a bakery in Tlaxiaco, told reporters that the boundaries favour bakeries near the state capital. The union said that other municipalities may apply to join after an evaluation.

What Comes Next

Labels carrying the new mark are expected in shops by October, ahead of the Day of the Dead season, when demand for pan de yema can triple. The state government has promised training on food safety and packaging for member bakeries, and a website listing certified producers is under construction.
