Opening Explorer in Mchezo Chess Trainer: Feature Documentation

Mchezo Chess Trainer is a training app developed in Nairobi for club players and school chess programmes across East Africa. This page documents the Opening Explorer, which lets users study openings move by move, see how often each move is played and how it scores, and build their own 
repertoire. It applies to version 2.3 of the app on And

roid, iOS and the web.

What the Explorer Shows When you open the Explorer, you see a board in the starting position and a table of possible moves. For each move, the table shows how many games in the database reached that position, the percentage won by White, drawn and won by Black, and the average rating of players who chose it. The database contains about 2.4 million games from online play and over-the-board tournaments, including 38,000 games from Kenyan, Ugandan and Ethiopian national events contributed by the federations.

You can switch between three databases using the selector above the table: Masters, which includes only players rated above 2200; All

Reef Restoration Nursery: How We Run It

This page belongs to the field operations space of the Projeto Coral Sul team, based in Arraial do Cabo. It explains how the coral nursery off the Prainha works, who does what, and the routines that keep the fragments alive. Updated by Guilherme Tavares on 21 September 2026.

Context

Arraial do Cabo sits in an unusual spot. Cold upwelling water reaches the coast here most summers, and the local reefs are built mainly by a handful of hardy species, especially Mussismilia hispida, rather than the richer communities of the northeast. Since 2024 we have grown fragments of this species in an underwater nursery and transplanted them to degraded patches on the Ilha de Cabo Frio reef, with permission from the federal marine reserve. We currently maintain 1,240 fragments on 31 frames.

Nursery Layout

The nursery is anchored in 8 metres of water on sand, about 150 metres from shore. Frames are steel tables raised 60 centimetres above the bottom, each holding forty fragments glued to ceramic plugs. They are arranged in four rows, labelled A to D, with buoys at each corner of the site. A temperature logger is attached to frame A1 and downloaded monthly.

Weekly Routine

Every Tuesday and Friday, weather permitting, two divers visit the nursery. Each visit covers the following tasks:

• Remove algae and sponges from the frames and plugs with soft brushes
• Check every fragment and note any that are pale, bleached or dead on the waterproof sheet
• Look for predators such as the fireworm, and remove them carefully with tongs
• Photograph two randomly chosen frames from above for the growth record
• Inspect anchor lines and buoys for wear

Dead fragments are removed so that they do not become sources of disease or algae. The sheet is transcribed into the shared spreadsheet the same day by whoever dived.

Transplanting

Fragments are transplanted once they reach about 6 centimetres in diameter, usually after ten to fourteen months. Transplant days are planned with Dra. Luana Moreira, who chooses the receiving sites and leads the dive. Fragments are fixed to the reef with marine epoxy, and each transplant site is tagged and visited after one, three and six months to measure survival.

Results So Far

Survival in the nursery over the last twelve months was 84 percent. Survival of transplanted fragments at six months is 71 percent, which is in line with similar projects elsewhere in Brazil. Losses were highest after a warm spell in March, when upwelling failed for three weeks and water temperature at the nursery reached 27.5 degrees.

Who to Ask

Questions about diving logistics go to Guilherme. Questions about coral health or research permits go to Dra. Moreira. Volunteers who want to help should first complete the induction session held on the first Saturday of each month.

Soil Science for Viticulture, Università di Udine, Master's Programme in Enology. Lecture 7 notes, prepared by the course tutor, Elisa Del Bianco. Session Focus: Soil pH, Lime and Iron Chlorosis in Vineyards Dr
 Franc
o Zuliani began by pointing out that vineyards in Friuli range from the strongly calcareous soils of the Carso, with pH above 8, to the acid flysch of the Collio, locally called ponca, where pH can fall below 6 in the subsoil. Rootstock choice, fertilisation and even grape variety depend on knowing where a vineyard sits on this scale, and growers who plant without proper soil tests often discover problems only after several years. What Soil pH Controls pH influences almost every chemical process in the root zone. In acid soils, aluminium and manganese become more soluble and can reach toxic levels, while phosphorus binds to iron and aluminium oxides. In alkaline soils, pho
sphorus binds to calcium instead, and iron, manganese, zinc and boron become less available. Microbial activity, including the breakdown of organic matter
 and nitrification, is generally highest between pH 6 and 7.5. Active Lime and Chlorosis

The key concept for calcareous soils is active lime, which is the fine fraction of calcium carbonate that dissolves readily and raises bicarbonate levels in the soil solution. High bicarbonate interferes with ir
on uptake and transport inside the vine, producing iron chlorosis: yellow leaves with green veins, starting on young
 shoots. Total carbonate is a poor predictor of chlorosis, and Dr Zuliani showed results from two Carso vineyards with the same total carbonate but very different active lime and very different chlorosis rates.

Steps to Assess Chlorosis Risk 1. Measure pH in water and in calcium chloride solution. 2. Determine total carbonate with a calcimeter. 3. Measure active lime by the Drouineau method using ammonium oxalate. 4. Measure extractable iron with DTPA. 5. Calculate the chlorosis potential index, which combines active lime and extractable iron. 6. Compare the index with the tolerance thresholds of candidate rootstocks. Rootstock Tolerance Rootstocks differ greatly in their tolerance. Riparia Gloire tolerates only about 6 percent active lime, the widely planted SO4 about 17 percent, 1103 Paulsen around 17 to 20 percent, and 140 Ruggeri and 41B up to 40 percent. Choosing a tolerant rootstock remains the most effective 
and cheapest way to prevent chlorosis, compared with repeated applications of iron chelates, which cost between 150 and 400 euros per hectare each year. Correcting Acidity

For acid soils on the Collio, liming is usually done before planting, mixing g
round limestone into the soil to the depth of the root zone. Correcting the subsoil after planting is very difficult. The required rate depends on buffer capacity, not only on pH, and can exceed ten tonnes per hectare on clay-rich flysch. Students should bring the soil analysis reports from the field trip to Cormons 
for the practical exercise next week.

In acid soils, aluminium and manganese become more soluble and can reach toxic levels, while phosphorus binds to iron and aluminium oxides. In alkaline soils, phosphorus binds to calcium instead, and iron, manganese, zinc and boron become less available. 1. Measure pH in water and in calcium chloride solution.
2. Determine total carbonate with a calcimeter.
3. Measure active lime by the Drouineau method using ammonium oxalate.

6. Compare the index with the tolerance thresholds of candidate rootstocks.

Rootstock Tolerance

Rootstocks differ greatly in their tolerance. Riparia Gloire tolerates only about 6 percent active lime, the widely planted SO4 about 17 percent, 1103 Paulsen around 17 to 20 percent, and 140 Ruggeri and 41B up to 40 percent. The required rate depends on buffer capacity, not only on pH, and can exceed ten tonnes per hectare on clay-rich flysch.

The Puniu River is a river of the Waikato region of New Zealand's North Island. As a tributary of the Waipā River (itself a tributary of the Waikato River), and at 
a length of , it is one of the longest secondary tributaries in New Zealand.

The Puniu flows initially north from sources within the Pureora Forest 
Park, veering northwest to pass south of the towns of Kihikihi and Te Awamutu before meeting the Waipā River south of Pirongia. Geology About half the river's course from its sources on the
edge of the Rangitoto Range is through deep valleys and gorges formed of Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous Manaia Hill Group greywacke (a form of sandstone, with little or no bedding, fine to medium grained, interbedded with siltstone and conglomerate, and with many quartz veins), which is buried in many places by Quaternary ignimbrites. The main ignimbrite is the Ongatiti Formation, up to 150 m thick of compound, weakly to strongly welded, vitrophyric, including pumice-, andesite and rhyolite lavas. In several places the river runs past slopes covered in blocks of ignimbrite, where the underlying greywacke has eroded.

For the remainder of its course, the river meanders over alluvium and colluvium to the Waipa. Initially these are mainly the Late Quaternary Piako Subgroup, which includes Late Pleistocene alluvium, and minor fan deposits of unconsolidated to v
ery soft, thinly to thickly bedded, yellow-grey to orange-brown, pumiceous mud, silt, sandy mud and gravel, with local muddy peat. Finally, the river flows mostly over the Holocene floodplain, where the alluvium and colluvium consist of variously coloured, unconsolidated sand, silt, mud, clay, local gravel and thin intercalated (a form of interbedding, where distinct deposits in close proximity migrate back and forth) peat beds. Vegetation The river 

rises in the Pureora Forest Park, before flowing past some unprotected remnants of rimu-tawa forest. In its lower reaches the river mostly flows through farmland, where the Puniu River Care Project is working on restoration of the river. Speed of flow In its final from Tokanui flows usually take 9 to 17 hours, depending on river levels. Pollution The Puniu is 6th dirtiest out of 13 sampling points in the Waipa catchment, with unsatisfactory nitrogen, phosphorus and turbidity levels. Puniu is the only river in Waikato with worsening ammonia levels.

Bridges
The river
originally had a seasonal ford near Kihikihi. The first bridge there was built about 1885, when the long railway bridge was also built. A ferro-concrete bridge replaced the old wooden bridge, downstream. It was largely built in 1936, completed in 1937 and still serves SH3.

See also List of rivers of New Zealand

The Wibault 313, Wibault Wib 313 or Penhoët Wibault Wib 313 was a single engine, single seat
 low wing monoplane fighter aircraft, designed and bu
ilt 
in France in the early 
1930s. It was entered into a government competitive tender programme but was not ordered. Design and development The Wib 313 was designed for the 1930 Service Technique de l'Aéronautique (S.T.Aé, Technical Department of Aeronautics) single-seat fighter (C.1) program

Fear Itself is a BBC Books original novel written by Nick Wallace and based on the long-running British science fiction television series Doctor Who. It features the Eighth Doctor, Fitz and Anji.

Synopsis
It is the twenty-second century and Earth is caught in a war with powerful alien forces. Paranoia runs rampant and the Doctor is in danger from all directions.

This was the only Past Doctor Adventure to feature the Eighth Doctor, as the original novels featuring that incarnation formed their own series, the Eighth Doctor Adventures. However, with the 2005 revival of the television series, and the BBC's New Series Adventures being published, the Eighth Doctor Adventures came to an end. By the time Fear Itself was released, Christopher Eccleston and David Tennant had made their debuts as the Ninth and Tenth incarnations of the Doctor, thus making the Eighth a "Past Doctor".

Summary of Legal Review: Proposed Structured Hiring Process for the City of Tempe Prepared by the Office of the City Attorney for the Human Resources Department, August 2026 Scope of Review Human Resources asked this office to assess whether the structured hiring process piloted in the Parks and Recreation division may be extended to all city departments without creating new exposure under federal and Arizona employment law. The pilot replaced unstructured panel interviews with standardized questions, scored rubrics and a blind fir
st-round review of applications. We reviewed the pilot handbook, the scoring forms, a sample o
f 64 completed hiring files, and the vendor contra
ct for the applicant tracking software.

Applicable Law The relevant authorities are Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Age Discrimination in Em
ployment Act, the Arizona Civil Rights Act, and the city's merit system rules. Arizona law also restricts inquiries into salary history for municipal positions, which became effective for the city in 2025, and the city's own ordinance prohibits questions about criminal history before a conditional offer. Findings
Overall, the structured process reduces legal risk compared with the previous practice, chiefly because it produces a written record linking each score to a job-related criterion. We did, however, identify several issues that should be corrected before expansion: - Two of
the standardized interview questions ask candidates about their availability on weekends 
in a way that could elicit information about religious
observance.
- The blind review removes names and addresses but leaves graduation years visible, which may permit inferences about age. - Rubric scores were changed after the panel meeting in five files without a documented reason. - The vendor contract does not require the software provider to retain records for the full period required by the merit system rules. - Reasonable accommodation requests are handled by email with no standard form, making response times hard to verify. Recommendations We recommend rewording the scheduling questions to describe the actual shift requirements and ask whether the candidate can meet them, with or without accommodation. Graduation years should be redacted alongside names. Any post-meeting score change should require a short written justification signed by the panel chair. The contract with the vendor should be amended to

require retention for at least four years after a position is filled, and Human Resources should adopt a standard accommodation request form. Conclusion Subject to these corrections, this office sees no legal obstacle to extending the structured process citywide. Please contact Assistant City Attorney Lorena Whitfield with any questions.

Summary of Legal Review: Proposed Structured Hiring Process for the City of Tempe

Prepared by the Office of the City Attorney for the Human Resources Department, August 2026

Scope of Review

Human Resources asked this office to assess whether the structured hiring process piloted in the Parks and Recreation division may be extended to all city departments without creating new exposure under federal and Arizona employment law. The pilot replaced unstructured panel interviews with standardized questions, scored rubrics and a blind first-round review of applications. We reviewed the pilot handbook, the scoring forms, a sample of 64 completed hiring files, and the vendor contract for the applicant tracking software.

Applicable Law

The relevant authorities are Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the Arizona Civil Rights Act, and the city's merit system rules. Arizona law also restricts inquiries into salary history for municipal positions, which became effective for the city in 2025, and the city's own ordinance prohibits questions about criminal history before a conditional offer.

Findings

Overall, the structured process reduces legal risk compared with the previous practice, chiefly because it produces a written record linking each score to a job-related criterion. We did, however, identify several issues that should be corrected before expansion:
- Two of the standardized interview questions ask candidates about their availability on weekends in a way that could elicit information about religious observance.
- The blind review removes names and addresses but leaves graduation years visible, which may permit inferences about age.
- Rubric scores were changed after the panel meeting in five files without a documented reason.
- The vendor contract does not require the software provider to retain records for the full period required by the merit system rules.
- Reasonable accommodation requests are handled by email with no standard form, making response times hard to verify.

Recommendations

We recommend rewording the scheduling questions to describe the actual shift requirements and ask whether the candidate can meet them, with or without accommodation. Graduation years should be redacted alongside names. Any post-meeting score change should require a short written justification signed by the panel chair. The contract with the vendor should be amended to require retention for at least four years after a position is filled, and Human Resources should adopt a standard accommodation request form.

Conclusion

Subject to these corrections, this office sees no legal obstacle to extending the structured process citywide. Please contact Assistant City Attorney Lorena Whitfield with any questions.

Technical Report SR-26-08: Rooftop Photovoltaic Retrofit at Gimhae Logistics Centre, Building C Prepared by Daehan Solar Engineering for the facilities department of Nara Freight Co., Ltd. Lead engineer: Yang Ji-ho. Review: Tran Minh Duc, PE. 1 Purpose and Scope This report documents the design, installation and first sixty days of operation of a 742-kilowatt peak rooftop photovoltaic system on Building C, a 14,800 square metre steel-framed warehouse completed in 2011. The project aims to supply the building's daytime cold storage load, reduce peak demand charges and qualify the site for the renewable energy
certificate scheme operated by the Korea Energy Agency. 2 Structural Assessment Before design began, the team commissioned a structural review because the roof was not originally specified for solar loads. The review found that the purlins could carry an additional 18 kilograms per square metre, provided the array avoided 
the two bays above the former mezzanine, where corrosion had reduced section thickness. The final layout therefore leaves those bays empty, which reduced the planned capacity from 810 to 742 kilowatts peak. 3 System Configuration The installed system consists of 1,325 bifacial monocrystalline modules rated at 560 watts each, mounted on a low-profile aluminium rail system clamped to the standing-seam roof without penetrations. Strings feed six 125-kilowatt
 string inverters located in a ventilated enclosure at ground level on the north wall. The point of connect
ion is the existing 22.9-kilovolt substation, through a new low-voltage panel and a dedicated meter for certificate reporting. 4 Installation Sequence Work proceeded over 38 
days in the following order: 1. Install temporary edge 
protection and safety lines along the full roof perimeter. 2. Mark rail positions using a laser level and verify clamp spacing against the structural drawing. 3. Fix rails and lift modules by crane in pallets of 31, distributing pallets across the roof to avoid point loads. 4. Mount modules row by row, connecting strings and labelling each cable at both ends. 5. Run DC cables in covered trays to the inverter enclosure and perform insulation resistance tests. 6. Commission inverters, verify protection settings with KEPCO, and energise the
system. 5 Early Performance

Over the first sixty days, from 20 July to 17 September, the system generated 186.4 megawatt-hours, about 4 percent above the simulation estimate for the period. The surplus is attributed to bifacial gain from the light-grey roof membrane, which reflects more light onto module rear surfaces than the simulation assumed. Peak demand at the site fell from 1.38 to 1.02 megawatts on clear days, though cloudy days showed little reduction, as expected. 6 Issues and Recommendations Two inverters tripped on high DC voltage during cool, clear mornings in early September. The strings feeding them were reconfigured from 28 to 27 modules, and no further trips have occurred. Module soiling from nearby truck traffic is heavier than anticipated, and we recommend cleaning twice yearly rather than once. A full annual performance review will be issued in July 2027.

A-Train aka Jeongseon Arirang A-Train () is a South Korean tourist train operated by Korail. The train began operations in 2015 and transports tourists through Jeongseon County in central Gangwon-do.

Overview

The train opened on January 22, 2015, from Cheongnyangni Station in northeastern Seoul and passes through several stations in Gangwon-do, including Mindungsan and Jeongseon, which hosts the "Jeongseon Five-day Market", and arriving at Auraji Station.

The "A" in the train's name comes from "Arirang" (a Korean folk song), and the words "amazement" and "adventure". The song has many variations, and the Jeongseon Arirang is a regional one. The song is listed as an Intangible Cultural Heritage by UNESCO and sometimes regarded as an unofficial anthem of Korea.

The train has four themed cars with large windows and glass walls; one is a sky room, one a tea room, and two of the cars are decorated in regional colors of red, yellow, blue and purple representing Jeongseon's geographical features such as the Dong River and the mountain ridges. The train's exterior includes a purple color for the pulsatilla, Jeongseon's official flower, and is decorated with curves that symbolize the Arirang melody. Activities on the train include storytelling, music, magic shows and quiz games.

The new line to Jeongseon is the first train to be named after a Korean town, and generated additional local interest due to the proximity of the scheduled 2018 Winter Olympics in Pyeongchang, a nearby town.

Operations

Started running: January 22, 2015
Stations: Cheongnyangni station - Mindungsan station - Byeoreogok station - Sonpyong station - Jeongseon station - Najeon station - Auraji station

Item Records in the Law School Library Catalogue

Maintained by the technical services team, Sungkyunkwan University Law School Library. Page owner: Jun Hye-sun. Last reviewed after the September semester start.

This page describes how we create and edit item records in the catalogue for print materials, especially the loose-leaf services, statute compilations and multi-volume treatises that make up most of the law collection. It is aimed at new staff and student assistants. Bibliographic records, which describe the work as a whole, are covered separately on the cataloguing standards page; this page deals only with item records, which describe the physical copies we hold.

Why Item Records Matter Here

Law materials change constantly. A single treatise on the Korean Civil Code may have twelve volumes, each updated with replacement pages several times a year. If item records are inaccurate, students cannot tell which volume is on the shelf or whether a compilation is current, and the library loses track of expensive subscriptions. During last year's inventory, about 7 percent of item records in the statutes section did not match the physical volumes, mostly because updates had been filed without the records being edited.

Fields to Complete for Every Item

* Barcode, scanned from the label applied to the inside back cover, never typed by hand.
* Volume number, using arabic numerals even when the spine shows roman numerals.
* Supplement or update date, recorded as YYYY-MM for loose-leaf services.
* Location code, such as LAW-REF for reference shelves or LAW-RES for reserve.
* Loan type, which determines whether the item can leave the building.
* A public note when the item is incomplete or missing pages.

Handling Updates to Loose-Leaf Services

When replacement pages arrive, file them in the binder first, then open the item record and change the supplement date. If the update includes a new tab or section, add a public note so that readers know the binder has expanded. Do not create a new item record for an update; that inflates our counts and confuses circulation statistics. Student assistant Ngo Thanh Truc wrote a short checklist for this process, which is taped to the filing desk.

Foreign Law Materials

We also hold a growing collection on Vietnamese law to support the school's exchange programme with Hanoi Law University. Vietnamese titles should be catalogued with full diacritics in the bibliographic record. For item records, the main difference is the location code LAW-ASIA. Ms. Le Phuong Thao, our Vietnamese-speaking cataloguer, is the contact for these materials.

Common Errors and How to Fix Them

Duplicate barcodes usually mean a label was printed twice; check both items and relabel one. Items showing as on loan but found on the shelf need a check-in scan before anyone edits them. If you are unsure about any change, ask in the technical services channel before saving.

Measles Vaccine Drive Reaches Riverside Communities Along the Rio Negro BARCELOS, Amazonas — For three weeks in September, a converted riverboat named Esperança do Rio carried two nurses, a doctor, a pharmacist and some 4,000 doses of vaccine up the Rio Negro, stopping at riverside communities that have no permanent health post. By the time it returned to Barcelos on Sunday, the team had vaccinated 2,317 people, most of them children under ten. The voyage was part of a state campaign launched after Amazonas recorded 46 confirmed measles cases between January and July, the highest number since the outbreak of 2018. Health authorities say coverage with the second dose of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine in some rural municipalities has fallen below 60 percent, far short of the 95 percent needed to prevent outbreaks. Lif
e on Board The boat set out from Barcelos on 2 September with refrigerators powered by a diesel generator and solar panels on the roof. Nurse Adriana Pimentel, who has worked on river health missions for twelve years, said keeping the vaccines between 2 and 8 degrees was the hardest part. "When it is 36 degrees outside and the generator stops at night, you sleep beside the thermometer," she said.

At each stop, community health agents who live in the villages had already prepared lists of children due for vaccination. The team set up under a tree or in the local school, 
and families arrived by canoe from surrounding settlements. What the Team Delivered

According to the state health secretariat, the boat provided:

- 1,486 doses of measles, mumps and rubella vaccine - 512 doses of yellow fever vaccine - 319 doses of other vaccines from the routine childhood schedule - Update
d vaccination records for more than 900 families Obstacles 
Remain The low water season complicated the trip. On two occasions the boat could not reach communities on side channels, and the team travelled the last stretch in smaller aluminium boats. Dr. Marcelo Quaresma, who led the mission, said that two communities could not be reached at all and will be visited in November when water levels rise. Hesitancy was less of a problem than distance, he said, though some parents had heard rumours on social media that the vaccine caused fevers that could harm children. "Most of them only needed someone they trust to explain it face to face," he said. Next Steps A second boat will cover communities along the Rio Branco in October, and the secretariat plans to repeat the Rio Negro trip in March t
o deliver second doses. Health secretary Dra. Cláudia Lins said the campaign cost about R$ 1.2 million, a fraction of what a widespread outbreak would cost the health system in hospital care.

BARCELOS, Amazonas — For three weeks in September, a converted riverboat named Esperança do Rio carried two nurses, a doctor, a pharmacist and some 4,000 doses of vaccine up the Rio Negro, stopping at riverside communities that have no permanent health post. By the time it returned to Barcelos on Sunday, the team had vaccinated 2,317 people, most of them children under ten.

Health authorities say coverage with the second dose of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine in some rural municipalities has fallen below 60 percent, far short of the 95 percent needed to prevent outbreaks.

Nurse Adriana Pimentel, who has worked on river health missions for twelve years, said keeping the vaccines between 2 and 8 degrees was the hardest part. "When it is 36 degrees outside and the generator stops at night, you sleep beside the thermometer," she said.

At each stop, community health agents who live in the villages had already prepared lists of children due for vaccination. The team set up under a tree or in the local school, and families arrived by canoe from surrounding settlements.

According to the state health secretariat, the boat provided:

- 1,486 doses of measles, mumps and rubella vaccine
- 512 doses of yellow fever vaccine

Cláudia Lins said the campaign cost about R$ 1.2 million, a fraction of what a widespread outbreak would cost the health system in hospital care.

David John Dalling (1939 – 1 August 2020) was a South African politician, lawyer, and political commentator. He served in the apartheid-era House of Assembly from 1974 to 1994, representing the Sandton constituency. He later represented the African National Congress (ANC) in the National Assembly from 1994 to 1999.

In the House of Assembly, Dalling represented the United Party, the Progressive Federal Party, and the Democratic Party, and then spent his last two years as an independent after publicly declaring his support for the ANC in 1992. After his term as an ANC representative, he terminated his membership in the party, and he joined the Congress of the People in 2009.

Early life and career
Born in 1939, Dalling was educated at Pretoria Boys High School, where he was head boy in 1957. He also played inter-provincial rugby until a hamstring injury prematurely ended his athletic career. After completing his undergraduate at Wits University, he practiced as an attorney. He entered frontline politics in 1967, when he was elected to represent his political party, the United Party, as a city councillor in the City of Johannesburg. He later represented the UP in the Transvaal provincial legislature.

House of Assembly: 1974–1994
In 1974, Dalling was elected to the House of Assembly, representing the UP in the wealthy constituency of Sandton, Johannesburg. After the collapse of the UP, Dalling was a member of the Progressive Federal Party and later of the Democratic Party (DP).

In 1987, Dalling was censured as an MP for remarks he made in the chamber about the Munnik Commission, an inquiry which had prepared the ground for parliamentary action against First National Bank by finding that the bank had helped finance an advertising campaign calling for the unbanning of the anti-apartheid African National Congress (ANC). During a parliamentary debate, Dalling alleged that the chairperson of the commission, Cape Judge President George Munnik, had a conflict of interest insofar as he was a supporter of the governing National Party and insofar as his own bank accounts had been closed by First National Bank. Dalling said that the commission's report was "a travesty of justice initiated by the state president", remarks which Minister of Justice Kobie Coetsee said constituted "gutter politics of the worst sort".

In 1990, after the ANC was unbanned during the negotiations to end apartheid, Dalling publicly advocated for his party, the DP, to forge a multi-racial alliance with the ANC. Later the same year, Dalling was subject to a Stratcom operation by the police's Security Branch: the Star printed a copy of a cheque, apparently signed by Dalling, for ANC membership fees. Policeman Paul Erasmus later admitted that the original cheque had been signed by Dalling's wife, for her own ANC membership, and that Dalling's signature had been forged.

However, in April 1992, Dalling did in fact join the ANC. With four other DP parliamentarians – Jannie Momberg, Pierre Cronjé, Jan van Eck, and Robert Haswell – he announced that he was defecting from the DP to join the ANC. In a joint statement, the group said that they were responding to a call made by Nelson Mandela shortly after his release from prison in 1990, for "all our white compatriots to join us in the shaping of a new South Africa". Dalling and the others remained in the House of Assembly as independents for the rest of the parliamentary term.

Migration Changelog: Patient Records System, Landesklinikum Wiener Neustadt

This log tracks each step of moving the hospital's patient administration database from the legacy Sybase server to Microsoft SQL Server 2022. It is kept by the database team under Martina Haberfellner and shared with ward administrators so they know what to expect after each maintenance window. Entries are in reverse order.

Step 5, completed 8 November 2025

- Switched all read and write traffic for outpatient appointments to the new server.
- Disabled write access to the corresponding tables on the old server.
- Rebuilt full-text indexes for referral letters.
- Removed the nightly replication job for the outpatient schema.

This was the first step where the new system became the sole source of truth for a business area. Outpatient appointments were chosen because they involve fewer integrations than inpatient admissions and because errors are easier to correct by phone with patients. The rebuild of full-text indexes was necessary because referral letter searches by diagnosis keywords returned incomplete results during the trial week. The cause was a difference in how the two database systems handle German compound words, and the team configured a German word breaker on the new server to fix it.

Step 4, completed 18 October 2025

- Ran the outpatient module in parallel on both servers for seven days.
- Compared 41,000 records daily using checksum scripts.
- Fixed 23 discrepancies caused by date fields with time zone offsets.

Parallel running doubled the load on the integration engine, so the window was kept short. The date discrepancies stemmed from appointments created during the switch from summer to winter time in 2019, when an old interface had stored times inconsistently. Robert Fasching from the clinical informatics team corrected them manually after checking each one against the paper appointment books, which the outpatient clinic still keeps.

Step 3, completed 27 September 2025

- Migrated reference data such as departments, physicians and insurance carriers.
- Mapped 312 legacy insurance codes to the current codes used by the Austrian health insurance fund.

The legacy system contained insurance codes for carriers that had merged in the 2020 social insurance reform, when nine regional funds were combined into one. Leaving them unmapped would have caused billing rejections.

Steps 1 and 2, completed August 2025

- Provisioned the new server cluster and configured nightly backups to the secondary data centre in Baden.
- Copied historical records from before 2015 as read-only archive tables.

What Comes Next

Inpatient admissions and discharge data will move in step 6, planned for the weekend of 17 January 2026, when bed occupancy is typically lowest. Ward staff will receive a one-page guide at least two weeks beforehand. During the eight-hour cutover, admissions will be recorded on paper forms and entered afterwards by the night administration team.

Albert Pike (December 29, 1809April 2, 1891) was an American author, poet, orator, editor, lawyer, jurist and Confederate States Army general who served as an associate justice of the Arkansas Supreme Court in exile from 1864 to 1865. He had previously served as a senior officer of the Confederate States Army, commanding the District of Indian Territory in the Trans-Mississippi Theater. A prominent member of the Freemasons, Pike served as the Sovereign Grand Commander of the Supreme Council, Scottish Rite (Southern Jurisdiction, USA) from 1859 to 1891.

Early life and education Albert Pike was born in Boston, Massachusetts, on December 29, 1809, the son of Benjamin and Sarah (Andrews) Pike, and spent his childhood in Byfield and Newburyport, Massachusetts. His colonial ancestors settled the area in 1635, and included John Pike (1613–1688/1689), the founder of Woodbridge, New Jersey. He attended school in Newburyport and Framingham until he was 15. In August 1825, he passed entrance exams at Harvard University, though when the college requested payment of tuition fees for the first two years, he chose not to attend. He began a program of self-education, later becoming a schoolteacher in Gloucester, North Bedford, Fairhaven and Newburyport. Pike was an imposing figure; tall and with hair that reached his shoulders and a long beard. In 1831, he left Massachusetts to travel west, first stopping in Nashville, Tennessee, and later moving to St. Louis, Missouri. There he joined a hunting and trading expedition to Taos, New Mexico. En route his horse broke and ran, forcing Pike to walk the remaining to Taos. After this, he joined a trapping expedition to the Llano Estacado in New Mexico and Texas. Trapping was minimal and, after traveling about , half of it on foot, he finally arrived at Fort Smith, Arkansas. Career

Settling in Arkansa
s in 1833, Pike taught in a school and wrote a series of articles for the Little Rock Arkansas Advocate under the pen name of "Casca." The articles were sufficiently well received for him to be asked to join the newspaper's staff. Under Pike's administration, the Advocate promoted the viewpoint of the Whig Party in a politically volatile and divided Arkansas in December 1832. After marrying Mary Ann Hamilton in 1834, he purchased the newspaper. He was the first reporter for the Arkansas Supreme Court. He wrote a book (published anonymously), titled The Arkansas Form Book, which was a guidebook for lawyers. Pike began to study law and was admitted to the bar in 1837, selling the Advocate the same year. (At least one source indicates that Pike read Kent and Blackstone and was admitted to the bar in 1834 by Superior Court judge Thomas J. Lacy, after a perfunctory examination.) He proved to be a highly effective lawyer, representing clients in courts at every level, which continued after he received permission to practice before the United States Supreme Court in 1849.

He also made several contacts among the Native American tribes in the area. He specialized in claims on behalf of Native Americans against the federal government. In 1852, he represented the Creek Nation before the Supreme Court in a claim regarding ceded tribal land. In 1854 he advocated for the Choctaw and Chickasaw, although compensation later awarded to the tribes in 1856 and 1857 was insufficient. These relationships were to influence the course of his Civil War service. He also began a campaign of newspaper essays urging support for the construction of a transcontinental railroad extending from New Orleans to the Pacific coast, moving to New Orleans in 1853 and preparing to pass the state bar in furtherance of his campaign, and was ultimately able to secure a charter from the Louisiana State Legislature for a project, following which he returned to Little Rock in 1857.

Policy Memorandum

To: Space Policy Committee members
From: Dr. Reiko Amano, space strategy secretariat
Subject: allocating rideshare launch slots

Summary

Demand from Japanese universities and start-ups for rideshare launch opportunities has grown faster than the domestic supply of slots. In fiscal 2025 the secretariat received 47 applications for government-supported rideshare places on domestic launches, but only 19 slots were available. Several teams waited more than two years, and three start-ups that had raised private funding chose foreign launch providers instead. This memo recommends changes to how slots are allocated, without requiring additional launches.

Current Arrangements

Slots on government launches are offered through an annual call. Proposals are scored by an expert panel on scientific merit, technological novelty and educational value, and the highest-scoring proposals receive slots on the next available flight. The process treats every proposal identically regardless of how ready the satellite is, so selected teams sometimes miss their assigned flight because hardware is not finished, leaving the slot unused or filled at short notice.

Recommendations

1. Introduce a readiness gate requiring a successful environmental test of the flight model before a slot is firmly assigned
2. Create a reserve list of ready satellites that can fill slots vacated by teams who miss their gate
3. Reserve a fixed share of slots, around 40 percent, for first-time university teams
4. Publish a rolling three-year schedule of expected rideshare opportunities to improve planning
5. Allow start-ups to purchase unused slots at cost when no qualified reserve satellite is available

Expected Effects

Based on the past three years, we estimate that a readiness gate and reserve list would have filled at least six slots that went unused or were filled by ballast mass. Reserving places for first-time university teams protects the educational function of the programme, which has trained many of the engineers now working at domestic satellite companies. Allowing paid use of unused slots would generate modest revenue and keep start-ups using domestic launches, which supports the long-term viability of the launch industry in Kagoshima and Hokkaido.

Risks

A readiness gate could disadvantage teams with less access to testing facilities. To address this, the secretariat recommends expanding access to environmental test equipment at the Tsukuba and Sagamihara facilities, with a modest budget for travel and facility time for university teams. Consultation with the space agency and launch providers should take place before the committee's December meeting.

1. Introduce a readiness gate requiring a successful environmental test of the flight model before a slot is firmly assigned
2. Create a reserve list of ready satellites that can fill slots vacated by teams who miss their gate
3. Reserve a fixed share of slots, around 40 percent, for first-time university teams
4. Publish a rolling three-year schedule of expected rideshare opportunities to improve planning
5. Allow start-ups to purchase unused slots at cost when no qualified reserve satellite is available

Expected Effects

Based on the past three years, we estimate that a readiness gate and reserve list would have filled at least six slots that went unused or were filled by ballast mass. Reserving places for first-time university teams protects the educational function of the programme, which has trained many of the engineers now working at domestic satellite companies. Allowing paid use of unused slots would generate modest revenue and keep start-ups using domestic launches, which supports the long-term viability of the launch industry in Kagoshima and Hokkaido.

Risks

A readiness gate could disadvantage teams with less access to testing facilities. To address this, the secretariat recommends expanding access to environmental test equipment at the Tsukuba and Sagamihara facilities, with a modest budget for travel and facility time for university teams. Consultation with the space agency and launch providers should take place before the committee's December meeting.

 the company said on Thursday. The farm, one of Kenya's oldest commercial wind projects, has a mix of turbines installed between 2009 and 2015 along the ridge overlooking Nairobi. By mid-2025, nine of its turbines were out of service because of mechanical problems, reducing the farm's output by roughly a third. Re
sidents of nearby villages had grown used to seeing several turbines standing still even on windy days.

KenGen's general manager for renewable energy, Eng. Purity Wanjala, said the repairs had taken longer than planned because replacement gearboxes had to be ordered from Europe and shipped through Mombasa. "These are older machines, and parts are not always on the shelf," she said. "We have now replaced four gearboxes, repaired blades on six turbines, and upgraded the control systems on all of them." What the Repairs Involved

- Upgrading turb

Wanjala said the vibration sensors were the most important long-term change. "In the past, we often found out a gearbox was failing only when it stopped," she said. "Now we can see 
the warning signs weeks in advance and plan repairs before a breakdown."

Local Jobs

rent level," she said. Looking

tation of the federal Medicaid program serving low-income individuals, including families, seniors, persons with disabilities,

and childless adults with incomes below 138% of federal poverty level. Benefits include ambulatory patient services, emergency services, hospitalization, maternity and newborn care, mental health and substance

use disorder treatment, dental (Denti-Cal), vision, and long-term care and support. Approximately 15.28 million people were enrolled in Medi-Cal as of September 2022, or about 40% of California's population; in most counties, more than half of eligible residents were enrolled as of 2020.  and children, pregnant women, persons in a skilled nursing or inter
mediate care home, and persons in the Breast and Cervical Cancer Trea
tment Program (BCCTP). People receiving federally funded cash assistance programs, such as CalWORKs (a state implementation of the federal Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program), the State Supplementation Program (SSP) (a state supplement to the federal Supplemental Security Income (SSI) program), foster care, adoption assistance, certain refugee assistance programs, or In-Home Supportive Services (IHSS) are also eligible. As a means-tested program, Medi-Cal imposes asset limits on certain prospective enrollees.
 Medi-Cal individuals who receive long-term supportive services or who enroll in Medi-Cal through certain disabilities are subject to asset tests. This limit depends on the number of individuals being considered for coverage; for one enrollee, this limit is $2,000, while for two enrollees, the limit is $3,000. Fyodor Vasilyevich Lopukhov (; 20 October 1886, Saint Petersburg – 28 January 1973, Leningrad) was a Soviet and Russian ballet dancer and choreographer. People's Artist of the RSFSR (1956). Training and dance career Lopukhov was born into a family of dancers, which included his brother, Andrei, and his two sisters, Evgenia and the renowned Lydia Lopokova. To re-appeal to the public, choreographers in Soviet Russia explored new performance spaces and formed smaller chamber ballet companies where there would be more scope for creativity. elusive group. Th
e second “process” depicts dissatisfied citizens with robbers and drunks who are defeated by the working class. Some other ballets choreographed by Lopukhov in an effort to
find a new means of expression include Night on Bald Mountain, with music by Mussorgsky (1924), Pulcinella (1926) and The Fox (1927), both with music by Stravinsky. His attempts to evolve the principles of classical dance were displayed in the acrobatic movements and character dances closely resembling the original ethnic dances they sprung forth from. Alexander "Ali" Marpet (; born April 17, 1993) is an American former professional football guard who played seven seasons for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers of the National Football League (NFL). Marpet played college football at Hobart and William Smith Colleges, a small liberal arts college with an enrollment of 2,271. In 2014, he was a Lindy's preseason All-American first-team, American Football Coaches Association (AFCA) All-American, D3football.com All-America first-team, and Liberty League Co-Offensive Player of the Year.

He attended the 2015 Senior Bowl, as the first NCAA Division III player picked to play in the all-star game in 25 years. Sports Illustrated named Marpet the "biggest riser" at the game, and include
d him on its All-Offense team. At the Scouting Combine in February 2015, he ran the fastest 40-yard dash among offensive line prospects eligible for the 2015 NFL Draft (4.98), the fastest split (1.74 seconds), and also the second-best time in the three-cone drill (7.33) and 20-yard shuttle (4.47), while scoring the highest "Speed, Power, Agility, Reaction and Quickness" (SPARQ) score. He also performed 30 repetitions at in the bench press, tied for fifth-best among offensive linemen. He also had a vertical leap of greater than 30 inches, and a Wonderlic test intelligence score of over 30. Drafted in the second round, 61st overall, of the 2015 NFL draft by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, Marpet is the highest-drafted pick in the history of NCAA Division III football. Early life Marpet grew up in Hastings-on-Hudson, New York. The village is in Westchester County, northeast of New York City.

His father, Bill Marpet, is an Emmy Award-winning videographer and director who since 1993 has headed B Productions, and produces fashion videos in New York. Ali Marpet's mother is Joy Rose. She was in a rock band called "Housewives on Prozac," and founded the Mamapalooza music and arts festival and the popup museum Museum of Motherhood. His parents are divorced. Ali has three siblings: two older brothers, Blaze and Brody, and a younger sister, Zena.

Marpet, who is Jewish, is an alumnus of Birthright Israel. Marp
et said that it would be a "huge honor" to represent Jews as an athlete. Marpet joined then-current Jewish National Football League (NFL) offensive linemen Geoff Schwartz, Mitchell Schwartz, Adam Bisn
owaty and Gabe Carimi. High school career At Hastings High School, Marpet played offensive tackle and defensive end for the Yellowjackets, was a three-time varsity letterman, named second-team All-State, earned all-section honors, and was a two-time all-league selection. He played the offensive line as a
 ninth-grader. Marpet quit playing football after his freshman year to focus on basketball where he earned all-league selection twice. Marpet rejoined the football team in his junior year, by which time he weighed . Marpet helped lead the Hastings squad to the section finals in 2010. Hastings lost to Bronxville, the eventual state champions. College career

Hobart College Marpet attended Hobart College, subsequent to being sought after to play football by Holy Cross, Fordham University, and Marist College. He graduated with a bachelor's degree in economics and a minor in philosophy and public policy in spring 2015. Hobart is a small private liberal arts college of 2,271 students in Geneva, in Upstate New York. The school competes in NCAA Division III, which does not award athletic scholarships. Only one other Hobart football player was drafted by the NFL before Marpet—in 1937, when halfback Fred King was drafted and ultimately played one game for the NFL's Brooklyn Dodgers. Marpet was not highly recruited out of high school by larger collegiate programs. He weighed as a
 freshman, increased his weight to by sophomore year, and by his junior year by eating a 7,000–9,000 calories a day diet. He originally wanted to play both basketball and football in college.

input: Pig Island is a small island in far north Queensland, Australia 19 km North East of Cape Grenville in the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Queensland, Australia and is part of the Cockburn Islands Group. It is around 160 hectares or 1.6 square km in size. It is to the north of Bootie Island, Manley Islet and Buchen Rock within the Cockburn Reef adjacent to Pollard Channel and next to the Sir Charles Hardy Islands.

Rope Access Technicians in Short Supply as Burgenland's Turbines Ag
e NEUSIEDL AM SEE. On a windy Thursday in February, Christina Wendelin hangs from two ropes about 90 metres above a field near Gols, inspecting the leading edge of a rotor blade with a torch and a tablet. A thin crack has formed where the blade's protective coating meets its fibreglass shell, and she photographs it from three angles before descending. "Rain at 250 kilometres per hour wears down anything," she says on the ground, pointing at the blade tip. "We see this on almost every turbine older than ten years." Wendelin, 31, is one of roughly 40 rope access technicians based in eastern Austria who specialise in wind turbine blades. Demand for their work has risen sharply as the hundreds of turbines installed in Burgenland and Lower Austria between 2005 and 2015 reach middle age. Blade damage that was rare in
the first years of operation is now common, and operators are s
crambling to find people who can do the repairs.

A Growing Workload According to the Austrian wind energy association, Burgenland alone has more than 450 turbines, and nationwide the number exceeds 1,400. Most need a blade inspection every one or two years, and technicians say
the same few problems account for nearly all of their rep
air work: - Leading edge erosion from rain,
hail and insects, which can cut annual output by several percent if left untreated. - Lightning strikes that burn through receptors or crack the blade tip. - Cracks in the adhesive bond joining the two blade halves. - Damaged vortex generators and trailing edge serrations added for efficiency or noise reduction. Gerhard Stockinger, managing director of a blade service company in Parndorf, says his order book 
is full until the autumn. "Two years ago we had six technicians. Now we have fourteen and we still turn work away," he says. Training the Next Generation

Becoming a blade technician takes time. Candidates must complete rope access certification, a wind industry safety course, and specialised training in composite repair. Stockinger's company now runs its own training programme, which l
asts about four months. Qualified technicians typically earn between 3,200 and 4,500 euros gross per month, depending on experience and travel. The
work itself is physically demanding and seasonal. Repairs with resin and coatings require temperatures above about 10 degrees and dry weather, so most blade work takes place between April and October. Technicians work long days in summer and often spend weeks away from home on projects in Germany, Denmark or the Netherlands. Operators Look for Alternatives Some operators are testing drones for inspections, which can photograph a turbine's blades in under an hour without anyone leaving the ground. Robotic crawlers that sand and coat leading edges are also under development. Wendelin is not worried about being replaced. "The drone finds the damage," she says. "Someone still has to go up and fix it." The wind energy association estimates that eastern Austria will need at least 100 additional blade technicians by 2030 as turbine numbers continue to grow under the federal expansion targets.

Rope Access Technicians in Short Supply as Burgenland's Turbines Age

NEUSIEDL AM SEE. On a windy Thursday in February, Christina Wendelin hangs from two ropes about 90 metres above a field near Gols, inspecting the leading edge of a rotor blade with a torch and a tablet. A thin crack has formed where the blade's protective coating meets its fibreglass shell, and she photographs it from three angles before descending. "Rain at 250 kilometres per hour wears down anything," she says on the ground, pointing at the blade tip. "We see this on almost every turbine older than ten years."

Wendelin, 31, is one of roughly 40 rope access technicians based in eastern Austria who specialise in wind turbine blades. Demand for their work has risen sharply as the hundreds of turbines installed in Burgenland and Lower Austria between 2005 and 2015 reach middle age. Blade damage that was rare in the first years of operation is now common, and operators are scrambling to find people who can do the repairs.

A Growing Workload

According to the Austrian wind energy association, Burgenland alone has more than 450 turbines, and nationwide the number exceeds 1,400. Most need a blade inspection every one or two years, and technicians say the same few problems account for nearly all of their repair work:

- Leading edge erosion from rain, hail and insects, which can cut annual output by several percent if left untreated.
- Lightning strikes that burn through receptors or crack the blade tip.
- Cracks in the adhesive bond joining the two blade halves.
- Damaged vortex generators and trailing edge serrations added for efficiency or noise reduction.

Gerhard Stockinger, managing director of a blade service company in Parndorf, says his order book is full until the autumn. "Two years ago we had six technicians. Now we have fourteen and we still turn work away," he says.

Training the Next Generation

Becoming a blade technician takes time. Candidates must complete rope access certification, a wind industry safety course, and specialised training in composite repair. Stockinger's company now runs its own training programme, which lasts about four months. Qualified technicians typically earn between 3,200 and 4,500 euros gross per month, depending on experience and travel.

The work itself is physically demanding and seasonal. Repairs with resin and coatings require temperatures above about 10 degrees and dry weather, so most blade work takes place between April and October. Technicians work long days in summer and often spend weeks away from home on projects in Germany, Denmark or the Netherlands.

Operators Look for Alternatives

Some operators are testing drones for inspections, which can photograph a turbine's blades in under an hour without anyone leaving the ground. Robotic crawlers that sand and coat leading edges are also under development. Wendelin is not worried about being replaced. "The drone finds the damage," she says. "Someone still has to go up and fix it."

The wind energy association estimates that eastern Austria will need at least 100 additional blade technicians by 2030 as turbine numbers continue to grow under the federal expansion targets.

An aircraft (: aircraft) is a vehicle that is able to fly by gaining support from the air. It counters the force of gravity by using either static lift or the dynamic lift of an airfoil, or, in a few cases, direct downward thrust from its engines. Common examples of aircraft include airplanes, helicopters, airships (including blimps), gliders, paramotors, and hot air balloons. The human activity that surrounds aircraft is called aviation. The science of aviation, including designing and building aircraft, is called aeronautics. Crewed aircraft are flown by an onboard pilot, whereas unmanned aerial vehicles may be remotely controlled or self-controlled by onboard computers. Aircraft may be classified by different criteria, such as lift type, aircraft propulsion (if any), usage and others. History

Flying model craft and stories of manned flight go back many centuries; however, the first manned ascent — and safe descent — in modern times took place by larger hot-air balloons developed in the 18th century. Each of the two World Wars led to great technical advances. Consequently, the history of aircraft can be divided into five eras: Pioneers of flight, from the earliest experiments to 1914. First World War, 1914 to 1918. Aviation between the World Wars, 1918 to 1939.
Second World War, 1939 to 1945. Postwar era, also called the Jet Age, 1945 to the present day.

Methods of lift Lighter than air – aerostats Aerostats use buoyancy to float in the air in much the same way that ships float on the water. They are characterized by one or more large cells or canopies, filled with a relatively low-density gas such as helium, hydrogen, or hot air, which is less dense than the surrounding air. When the weight of this is added to the weight of the aircraft structure, it adds up to the same weight as the air that the craft displaces.

Small hot-air balloons, called sky lanterns, were first invented in ancient China prior to the 3rd century BC and used primarily in cultural

celebrations, and were only the second type of aircraft to fly, the first being kites, which were first invented in ancient China over two thousand years ago (see Han Dynasty).

A balloon was originally any aerostat, while the term airship was used for large, powered aircraft designs — usually fixed-wing. In 1919, Frederick Handley Page was reported as referring to "ships of the air," with smaller passenger types as "Air yachts." In the 1930s, large intercontinental flying boats were also sometimes r
eferred to as "ships of the air" or "flying-ships". — though none had yet been built. The advent of powered balloons, called dirigible balloons, and later of rigid hulls allowing a great increase in size, began to change the way these words were used. Huge powered aerostats, characterized by a rigid outer framework and separate aerodynamic skin surrounding the gas bags, were produced, the Zeppelins being the largest and most famous. There were still no fixed-wing aircraft or non-rigid balloons large enough to be called airships, so "airship" came to be synonymous with these aircraft. Then several accidents, such as the Hindenburg disaster in 1937, led to the demise of these airships. Nowadays a "balloon" is an unpowered aerostat and an "airship" is a powered one. A powered, steerable aerostat is called a dirigible. Sometimes this term is applied only to non-rigid balloons, and sometimes dirigible balloon is regarded as the definition of an airship (which may then be rigid or non-rigid). Non-rigid dirigibles are characterized by a moderately aerodynamic gasbag with stabilizing fins at the back. These soon became known as blimps. During World War II, this shape was widely adopted for tethered balloons; in windy weather, this both reduces the strain on the tether and stabilizes the balloon. The nickname blimp was adopted along with the shape. In modern times, any small dirigible or airship is called a blimp, though a blimp may be unpowered as well as powered.

is an archeological site with the ruins of a Nara period Buddhist temple located in the Hongō neighborhood of the city of Mihara, Hiroshima, Japan. It was designated as a National Historic Site in 1978. History The Yokomi ruins are located at the northwestern foot of the mountains in the eastern part of Hiroshima Prefecture, where the Nashiwa River joins the Nuta River. The existence of an ancient temple ruins has been known from ancient roof tiles that have been excavated from a field on the east side of the current
Municipal Hongō Junior High School. The temple name 'Yokomi' come from local folklore that there was once a temple named 'Yokomi-dera' at this location, but the temple is not mentioned in any historical documentation, so its actual name and history are unknown. An archaeological excavation was conducted by the Hiroshima Prefectural Board of Education from 1971 to 1973. The foundations of the lecture hall, pagoda, and surrounding enclosure were discovered during the excavation. The lecture hall was a 7 x 4 bay building measuring 25.5 by 15.1 meters. The area of the temple is thought to be about 100 meters from east-to-west and about 80 meters from north-to-south. The total layout, including the location of the Main Hall is unclear, but evidence indicates that the temple had a peculiar layout in that it was orientated to the west rather than the south. A large number of roof tiles with t
he design of snowflakes have been excavated. This six-petal snowflake pattern has also been found at the site of the Yamato Wakakusa temple ruin, as well as at the Yamada-dera in Asuka, Nara. Various others patterns of tiles, including single petal lotus pattern (also known as a "flame pattern"), are common to roof tiles in the Hak
uhō period from the Yamato region. Other artifacts include Sue ware pottery and gilt-bronze ornamental metal fittings. In addition, a large amount of Yayoi pottery from around the first half of the 3rd century was found in the lower layers of the temple site. According to the results of the excavation, it is currently regarded as the oldest temple in Hiroshima Prefecture, and it seems to have been abolished around the latter half of the Nara period. The Umekidaira Kofun and Mitoshiro Kofun are located in the surrounding area suggested that there was exchange between the Yamato Kingdom in the Kinai region and the local ruling family. The site is approximately 2.5 kilometers west from JR West Hongō Station. Artifacts from the site are exhibited at the Hiroshima Prefectural Museum of History and Folklore.

Danny Kelly
(born 23 December 1956) is a British music journalist, sports presenter, and internet publisher. He is the former editor of the music weekly New Musical Express and Q magazine.

Early life Danny Kelly was born in Islington to Irish parents and attended Our Lady of Sacred Heart in Eden Grove and then St Aloysius College, Highgate. Kelly has worked in print and radio journalism for over thirty years. He began writing for New Musical Express in about 1983 and was its editor from the late 1980s to 1992. Kelly later edited the British music monthly, Q, and was awarded the title British Magazine Editor of the Year for his work there. He left in 1995. He also launched the sports monthly Total Sport. He often works in partnership with fellow sports fan and radio journalist Danny Baker, who is also an NME alumnus, having broadcast in both commercial and BBC radio. Career In the mid-1990s Kelly hosted Under the Moon, a live late-night television sports chat and entertainment show that often ran for three or more hours. In 1997, he founded the 365 Corporation, best known for the UK football website, Football365. In 2006, he helped launch Videojugs, a video up/download service that seeks to demonstrate all human knowledge on film. He also launched The Times''' first weekly podcast, The Game. He currently presents a radio sports show on BBC London and hosted a weekly football podcast with Danny Baker. The football podcast ended in December 2007. He has appeared in two films: Divorcing Jack and The Football Factory. Kelly spent a period of time commencing December 2007 as stand-in presenter for Hawksbee & Jacobs, Evening Kick Off and George Galloway on talkSPORT radio. He joined the station to front Lets kick the ball during Euro 2008 between 19:00–22:00 (BST/GMT) every weekday. Kelly signed a permanent contract in August 2008 with talkSPORT to front the same slot during the regular football season. Kelly often remarks that he played football
in his yo
uth on Hackney Marshes.

On 8 January 2011, Kelly allegedly referred to Rafael Benitez as a 'nonce' live on air during
 a radio broadcast whilst criticising the performance of Liverpool. Media regulator Ofcom received 130 complaints about the comments.

After several seasons presenting The Full Time Phone-In on Saturday nights up to 2020, and hosting a Sunday evening show 
with ex-Crystal Palace owner Simon Jordan, he currently presents a Monday evening show called the PressBox, where he and the football editor of The Sun, Sean Custis, are joined by a studio guest "to pick apart the stories that have been filling our back pages" and Trans-Euro Express on Sunday nights, a programme featuring European football. In 2013, Kelly and Danny Baker were announced as part of BT Sport's football coverage, hosting a Friday evening show. Since August 2021 he has presented a Tottenham Hotspur podcast, The View
 From The Lane, on the sports website The Athletic''. Personal life His long term partner is the journalist Alex Clark. They both relocated to Ireland in 2018, from where Kelly often broadcasts remotely. On 9 December 2021, he announced via his Twitter account that they had married.

He currently presents a radio sports show on BBC London and hosted a weekly football podcast with Danny Baker. The football podcast ended in December 2007. He has appeared in two films: Divorcing Jack and The Football Factory.

Kelly spent a period of time commencing December 2007 as stand-in presenter for Hawksbee & Jacobs, Evening Kick Off and George Galloway on talkSPORT radio. He joined the station to front Lets kick the ball during Euro 2008 between 19:00–22:00 (BST/GMT) every weekday. Kelly signed a permanent contract in August 2008 with talkSPORT to front the same slot during the regular football season. Kelly often remarks that he played football in his youth on Hackney Marshes.

On 8 January 2011, Kelly allegedly referred to Rafael Benitez as a 'nonce' live on air during a radio broadcast whilst criticising the performance of Liverpool. Media regulator Ofcom received 130 complaints about the comments.

After several seasons presenting The Full Time Phone-In on Saturday nights up to 2020, and hosting a Sunday evening show with ex-Crystal Palace owner Simon Jordan, he currently presents a Monday evening show called the PressBox, where he and the football editor of The Sun, Sean Custis, are joined by a studio guest "to pick apart the stories that have been filling our back pages" and Trans-Euro Express on Sunday nights, a programme featuring European football.

In 2013, Kelly and Danny Baker were announced as part of BT Sport's football coverage, hosting a Friday evening show.

Since August 2021 he has presented a Tottenham Hotspur podcast, The View From The Lane, on the sports website The Athletic''.

Personal life

His long term partner is the journalist Alex Clark. They both relocated to Ireland in 2018, from where Kelly often broadcasts remotely. On 9 December 2021, he announced via his Twitter account that they had married.

The alkali metals consist of the chemical elements lithium (Li), sodium (Na), potassium (K), rubidium (Rb), caesium (Cs), and francium (Fr). Together with hydrogen they constitute group 1, which lies in the s-block of the periodic table. All alkali metals have their outermost electron in an s-orbital: this shared electron configuration results in their having very similar characteristic properties. Indeed, the alkali metals provide the best example of group trends in properties in the periodic table, with elements exhibiting well-characterised homologous behaviour. This family of elements is also known as the lithium family after its leading element.

The alkali metals are all shiny, soft, highly reactive metals at standard temperature and pressure and readily lose their outermost electron to form cations with charge +1. They can all be cut easily with a knife due to their softness, exposing a shiny surface that tarnishes rapidly in air due to oxidation by atmospheric moisture and oxygen (and in the case of lithium, nitrogen). Because of their high reactivity, they must be stored under oil to prevent reaction with air, and are found naturally only in salts and never as the free elements. Caesium, the fifth alkali metal, is the most reactive of all the metals. All the alkali metals react with water, with the heavier alkali metals reacting more vigorously than the lighter ones.

All of the discovered alkali metals occur in nature as their compounds: in order of abundance, sodium is the most abundant, followed by potassium, lithium, rubidium, caesium, and finally francium, which is very rare due to its extremely high radioactivity; francium occurs only in minute traces in nature as an intermediate step in some obscure side branches of the natural decay chains. Experiments have been conducted to attempt the synthesis of element 119, which is likely to be the next member of the group; none were successful. However, ununennium may not be an alkali metal due to relativistic effects, which are predicted to have a large influence on the chemical properties of superheavy elements; even if it does turn out to be an alkali metal, it is predicted to have some differences in physical and chemical properties from its lighter homologues.

Most alkali metals have many different applications. One of the best-known applications of the pure elements is the use of rubidium and caesium in atomic clocks, of which caesium atomic clocks form the basis of the second. A common application of the compounds of sodium is the sodium-vapour lamp, which emits light very efficiently. Table salt, or sodium chloride, has been used since antiquity. Lithium finds use as a psychiatric medication and as an anode in lithium batteries. Sodium, potassium and lithium are essential elements, having major biological roles as electrolytes, and although the other alkali metals are not essential, they also have various effects on the body, both beneficial and harmful.

History

Sodium compounds have been known since ancient times; salt (sodium chloride) has been an important commodity in human activities, as testified by the English word salary, referring to salarium, money paid to Roman soldiers for the purchase of salt. While potash has been used since ancient times, it was not understood for most of its history to be a fundamentally different substance from sodium mineral salts. Georg Ernst Stahl obtained experimental evidence which led him to suggest the fundamental difference of sodium and potassium salts in 1702, and Henri-Louis Duhamel du Monceau was able to prove this difference in 1736. The exact chemical composition of potassium and sodium compounds, and the status as chemical element of potassium and sodium, was not known then, and thus Antoine Lavoisier did not include either alkali in his list of chemical elements in 1789.

Using the Departure Board App at Your Station

The departure board app, developed for De Lijn and NMBS by the Ghent studio Pixelwerk, puts the information from the yellow and blue station displays on your phone. It shows departures from any Belgian railway station and the bus and tram stops around it, updated every thirty seconds. This manual explains how to set the app up, how to read the departure list, and what to do when trains are disrupted.

Setting Up

After installing the app, you will be asked for permission to use your location. If you allow it, the app automatically opens the nearest station or stop. If you prefer not to share your location, type the name of a station in the search bar. You can save up to ten favourite stations or stops by tapping the star icon next to the name. Favourites appear on the home screen in the order you saved them; press and hold to rearrange them.

Reading the Departure List

Each line in the departure list shows several pieces of information:

• The planned departure time, followed by the expected delay in red if the train is running late
• The destination and the type of train, such as IC for Intercity or S for suburban
• The platform number, which turns orange if it has changed from the timetable
• A small icon showing whether the train has bicycle spaces and step-free access
• For buses and trams, the line number and the stop position at the station square

Tap any departure to see all intermediate stops with their expected times. This is useful when you want to know whether you will make a connection further along your journey.

During Disruptions

When trains are cancelled or diverted, a yellow banner appears at the top of the screen. Tap the banner to read the full message from the railway, including advice on alternative routes. The app does not plan alternative journeys itself; for that, use the journey planner of NMBS or De Lijn, which can be opened directly from the banner.

Cancelled departures remain visible in the list with a line through them for fifteen minutes, so that you can check what happened if you arrive at the station and your train is not shown on the platform.

Notifications

You can ask the app to notify you about a specific departure. Tap the bell icon on a departure, and the app will alert you if the train is delayed by more than five minutes, if the platform changes, or if it is cancelled. Notifications stop automatically after the departure time. Commuters can set recurring notifications for the same train on weekdays under Settings and then My Trains.

Help and Feedback

If the information in the app differs from the station displays, the station displays are leading. Please report such differences using Feedback in the menu, so that the team led by Wannes De Smet can investigate.
